title: Storing food safely: how microbes spoil it, and when to take extra care

summary.text: A small pot of dal cooked at night is usually fine in the morning. A wedding pot of the same dal, boiled just as well, can make a hundred guests ill. The big pot stays warm in the middle for many hours, and warm food is where microbes multiply fastest. Your child heaps hot rice in a bowl and spreads the same rice on a plate. They time how long the middle of each stays hot. They watch which microbes spoil bread, rice and lemon in sealed bags. They test whether rice that looks dry is dry enough to store. They also learn where each food keeps best, and which people, foods and days need extra care.
summary.art: A very large covered cooking vessel beside a small pot on a kitchen floor at night, with a faint wisp of steam still rising from under the lid of the large one.

intro.hook: Two pots of dal are boiled for the same time and covered. By morning the small pot is safe and the big pot may not be. What did the size of the pot change?
intro.text: Most people think that food is safe if it was cooked well and covered. Cooking kills most microbes, but a few kinds survive boiling as tough spores. When the food cools to a warm temperature, the spores wake up and multiply. How long the food stays warm then matters more than how well it was cooked. In this unit you time how long the middle of a heap of rice stays hot. You work out how many bacteria ten bacteria become in six hours at three temperatures. You find out which microbes spoil which foods, and how damp grain grows a mould that makes a poison. You also plan a meal for a baby, a grandmother and a pregnant aunt at one table.
intro.art: A child pushing a digital thermometer into the middle of a bowl heaped with steaming rice, with a flat plate of spread rice beside the bowl.

outcomes: I can name five ways food is lost in storage, and give a kitchen example of each.
I can explain how bacteria, yeasts and moulds spoil food, and which of them spoils which kind of food.
I can use a doubling table to explain why warm food must be eaten or chilled within two hours.
I can explain why a big or deep pot of food cools slowly, and how to cool food safely.
I can choose the right place to store grain, vegetables, milk and cooked food, and give the reason.
I can say which people, foods, weather and situations need extra care with food, and what to change.
I can run a fair test with times or daily records, and say what my results show.
I can tell how the mould poison aflatoxin was found, and say what people still argue about in storing food.

terms.meaning: A change that makes food unfit to eat. Microbes cause most spoilage of moist food.
terms.example: Dal that has turned sour and frothy has spoiled.
terms.art: A steel bowl of dal with froth on top and a hand holding the lid away.

terms.meaning: A living being too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria, yeasts and moulds are microbes.
terms.example: One drop of sour milk holds millions of microbes.
terms.art: A drop of milk on a spoon with a round zoom-in showing many tiny rod and ball shapes.

terms.meaning: Microbes made of one tiny cell each. They multiply by splitting in two. One of them is called a bacterium.
terms.example: Bacteria turn wet cooked rice slimy within a day or two in summer.
terms.art: A zoom-in circle showing one rod-shaped cell pinching into two.

terms.meaning: A fungus made of one cell. Yeasts eat sugar and make gas and alcohol.
terms.example: Yeasts make old fruit juice fizzy and puff up the packet.
terms.art: A puffed-up juice carton beside a zoom-in of round cells with small buds.

terms.meaning: A fungus that grows as fine threads over food and makes powdery spores. Moulds can grow on drier and sourer food than bacteria can.
terms.example: The green patch on an old lemon is a mould.
terms.art: A lemon with a round blue-green fuzzy patch and a white edge.

terms.meaning: The fine threads that make up the body of a mould. They grow into the food, deeper than the patch you see.
terms.example: Under the fuzzy spot on bread, hyphae have already spread through the slice.
terms.art: A cut-away slice of bread with a fuzzy spot on top and thin threads reaching down into the slice.

terms.meaning: A tiny, tough, resting cell. Mould spores float in air and start new moulds. The spores of some bacteria survive boiling.
terms.example: Spores of the bacterium Bacillus cereus survive in cooked rice and wake when the rice turns warm.
terms.art: A zoom-in of a rice grain with a few tiny oval capsules on its surface.

terms.meaning: A substance made by living cells that cuts or joins other substances. Microbes pour enzymes on to food to digest it outside their bodies.
terms.example: Enzymes from bacteria cut the protein in fish, and the cut pieces smell bad.
terms.art: A zoom-in of a rod-shaped cell beside a long chain being snipped into short pieces.

terms.meaning: A poison made by a living being. Some microbes leave toxins in food, and some toxins stay after cooking.
terms.example: Aflatoxin is a toxin made by a mould on damp groundnuts and maize.
terms.art: A groundnut shell split open with a patch of yellow-green powder on one nut.

terms.meaning: The range of temperature from about 5 to 60 degrees Celsius. Bacteria multiply in this range, fastest between 20 and 45 degrees.
terms.example: Dal on the counter in May sits in the danger zone.
terms.art: A thermometer drawn with the band from 5 to 60 degrees shaded and a pot of dal beside the band.

terms.meaning: The time a group of bacteria takes to become twice as many.
terms.example: In warm food some bacteria have a doubling time of 20 minutes.
terms.art: A row of dots growing from one to two to four to eight, with a small clock above each step.

terms.meaning: The waiting time before bacteria in a new place begin to multiply. They use it to get ready for the new food.
terms.example: Bacteria that land in fresh dal may wait an hour or more before they start doubling.
terms.art: A flat line on a graph that then bends sharply upward, with a clock beside the flat part.

terms.meaning: Food that spoils within hours or days unless it is kept cold. Perishable foods are moist and not very sour, salty or sweet.
terms.example: Milk, cooked rice, fish and cut fruit are perishable.
terms.art: A fridge shelf holding a milk packet, a covered bowl of rice and a plate of cut papaya.

terms.meaning: The length of time a food stays good when it is stored as the label says.
terms.example: Unopened carton milk has a shelf life of about six months.
terms.art: A milk carton on a shelf with a calendar page beside the carton.

terms.meaning: An unbroken line of cold places that carries food from the maker to the home.
terms.example: Milk is chilled at the village, in the tanker, at the dairy, in the van and in the shop fridge.
terms.art: A row of five linked pictures: a milk can, a tanker, a dairy, a van and a shop fridge, joined by a blue line.

terms.meaning: To heat a food for a short time to kill the microbes that cause disease. Pasteurised milk is heated to 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds.
terms.example: Pouch milk is pasteurised, so it still needs the fridge.
terms.art: A milk pouch with the word pasteurised printed on the front.

terms.meaning: Short for ultra-high temperature. The food is heated to about 140 degrees Celsius for a few seconds and packed in a germ-free carton.
terms.example: UHT milk keeps for months on a shelf until the carton is opened.
terms.art: A milk carton standing on a kitchen shelf, not in a fridge.

terms.meaning: Closed so well that no air or damp can get in or out.
terms.example: Atta in an airtight dabba stays dry through the monsoon.
terms.art: A steel dabba with a tight lid and raindrops on the window behind the dabba.

terms.meaning: The sharp, stale smell and taste of fat or oil that air, light and warmth have changed. Microbes are not needed for this.
terms.example: Groundnuts kept for a year in a warm, open jar smell rancid.
terms.art: An open glass jar of groundnuts on a sunny window sill.

terms.meaning: An insect or other animal who eats stored food. Rice weevils, flour beetles, moths and rats are storage pests.
terms.example: A rice weevil lays her eggs inside grains of rice.
terms.art: A few grains of rice with one small dark beetle with a long snout walking over the grains.

terms.meaning: To heat cooked food again before eating. Safe reheating makes the food steaming hot all the way through.
terms.example: Reheat leftover sambar until it bubbles, and stir the middle.
terms.art: A small pot of sambar bubbling on a stove with a ladle stirring the middle.

terms.meaning: More easily harmed than most people. Babies, pregnant women, old people and ill people are more vulnerable to unsafe food.
terms.example: A baby of eight months is vulnerable, so her food is made fresh.
terms.art: A baby in a grandmother's lap, with a pregnant woman sitting beside them at a meal.

explanations.concept: Five ways food is lost in storage
explanations.definition: Stored food is lost in five ways. Microbes eat it, or the food's own life goes on, or pests get in. Air and light change it, or water moves in or out.
explanations.description: Microbes are the first way. They eat moist food and leave it sour, slimy, smelly or mouldy. The second way is the food's own life. A potato or an onion is alive, so they sprout. A banana goes on ripening until it is soft and black. The third way is pests. Weevils, moths, ants and rats eat stored grain and leave droppings. The fourth way needs no living being. Air, light and warmth slowly change oil and fat until they smell rancid. The fifth way is water on the move. A biscuit takes in damp from the air and turns soft. A chapati loses water and turns hard. Each way needs its own answer, so a good storer first asks which way threatens this food.
examples: Sour dal: microbes ate the dal.
A sprouting onion: the onion's own life went on.
Small beetles in the atta: storage pests got in.
Old groundnuts with a sharp smell: air and warmth turned the oil rancid.
A soft biscuit in the monsoon: water moved in from the air.
explanations.art: A kitchen shelf with five things in a row: a bowl of frothy dal, a sprouting onion, a jar of atta with small beetles, an open jar of groundnuts and a bent, soft biscuit.

explanations.concept: How microbes spoil food: they digest it from outside
explanations.definition: Microbes pour enzymes on to food. The enzymes cut the food into small pieces, and the microbes soak the pieces up. What they leave behind is the spoilage we see and smell.
explanations.description: A microbe has no mouth. To eat, they release enzymes into the food around them. The enzymes cut starch into sugars, proteins into smaller pieces and fats into acids. The microbe takes in what they need. The rest stays in the food, with the wastes the microbe makes. Acids make the food sour. Gases make froth and puff up a packet. Pieces of cut protein give the smell of bad fish or bad eggs. Enzymes that cut the glue between plant cells turn a firm vegetable to mush. Many bacteria also make a sticky coat around themselves, and this is the slime on old food. So each sign of spoilage is the trace of one kind of feeding.
examples: Sour milk: bacteria turned milk sugar into acid.
A swollen juice packet: yeasts turned sugar into gas.
The smell of bad fish: bacteria cut the proteins into smelly pieces.
A soft, wet patch on a tomato: microbes cut the glue between the cells.
explanations.art: A zoom-in of rod-shaped cells on a food surface, with small arrows going out from the cells to chains in the food and other arrows bringing small pieces back.

explanations.concept: Bacteria, yeasts and moulds: which spoils which food
explanations.definition: Bacteria win on wet food that is not sour. Yeasts win on sweet or slightly sour liquid. Moulds win on food that is drier, sourer or saltier.
explanations.description: All three kinds of microbe are nearly everywhere, so the food decides who grows first. Bacteria multiply fastest, but they need plenty of free water and little acid. Cooked rice, dal, milk, fish and meat suit them. Yeasts stand more sugar and more acid than most bacteria, so they spoil fruit juice and old fruit. Moulds grow slowly, but they stand dryness, salt and acid better than the others. They also need air. So moulds take the food that bacteria cannot use: bread, chapati, lemons, jam and the top of a pickle. This is why wet rice turns slimy in a day, while bread grows fuzz after several days. Knowing who will come tells you how to store the food.
examples: Wet cooked rice in a bag: slimy and watery within two days, from bacteria.
Bread in a bag: fuzzy white, green or black spots after three to six days, from moulds.
A lemon: a blue-green mould patch after a week or more, and almost never slime.
explanations.art: Three clear bags in a row holding wet rice with slime, a bread slice with fuzzy spots and a lemon slice with a blue-green patch.

explanations.concept: One microbe after another: how milk spoils in turns
explanations.definition: Spoiling is often a line of different microbes. Each kind changes the food, and the change suits the next kind.
explanations.description: Leave raw milk in a warm place and watch what scientists have seen many times. First, bacteria that eat milk sugar multiply and make acid. The milk turns sour and sets. The acid then stops those same bacteria. Next come yeasts and moulds, who can live in acid. They slowly use the acid up. When the sourness falls, a third group arrives: bacteria who digest protein. Now the milk smells rotten. Ecologists call such a line of changes a succession. The same word is used when bare ground turns to grass, then bushes, then forest. A bowl of milk passes through its own succession in a week or two.
examples: Day 1: milk sugar bacteria multiply, and the milk turns sour.
Days 3 to 7: yeasts and moulds grow on the sour curd.
After that: protein-eating bacteria take over, and the smell turns rotten.
explanations.art: Three bowls of milk in a row labelled first, next and last: one set and sour, one with a mould skin, one grey and broken.

explanations.concept: Spoiled food and unsafe food are not the same
explanations.definition: Spoilage microbes change how food looks and smells. Many microbes and toxins that make people ill change nothing you can see or smell.
explanations.description: Your nose is good at finding spoilage. It picks up the acids and gases that large numbers of spoilage microbes make. But the bacteria that cause the worst illness often work in small numbers and make no smell. Some leave a toxin in the food. Reheating kills the bacteria, but some toxins stay. A mould on damp groundnuts or maize makes a toxin called aflatoxin, which cooking does not destroy. So there are two separate questions about any stored food. Has it spoiled? And has it been kept in a way that lets harmful microbes multiply? Only the second question protects you, and you answer it from the food's history: how warm, how long, how damp.
examples: Sour curd has changed a lot and is safe.
Rice kept warm all night can look and smell fine and still hold a toxin.
Groundnuts that are shrivelled, mouldy or bitter should be thrown away.
explanations.art: Two bowls of rice that look exactly the same, one with a small clock showing 1 hour and one with a clock showing 10 hours.

explanations.concept: Time and temperature: why two hours
explanations.definition: Bacteria multiply by doubling. How often they double depends on the temperature, so warmth and time together decide how many bacteria a food holds.
explanations.description: In warm food at about 35 degrees Celsius, some bacteria double every 20 minutes. Ten bacteria become 640 in two hours and more than two million in six hours. In a cool room at 18 degrees they may double only every two hours. In a fridge at 4 degrees most food bacteria stop. Bacteria also wait before they start. This waiting time is called the lag time, and it often lasts an hour or more in fresh food. The two-hour rule comes from these facts. Cooked food can stay in the danger zone, from 5 to 60 degrees, for about two hours in all. After that, eat it, chill it or keep it hotter than 60 degrees. On days hotter than about 32 degrees, food safety agencies shorten the time to one hour.
examples: Sambar served at 1 o'clock should be in the fridge by 3 o'clock.
A flask that keeps soup hotter than 60 degrees Celsius keeps the soup out of the danger zone.
The two hours add up: one hour on the table at lunch and one hour at dinner make two.
explanations.art: A line graph with three lines from the same starting point: one shooting steeply up, one rising gently and one staying flat, each with a small thermometer.

explanations.concept: Why a big pot stays warm in the middle
explanations.definition: Heat leaves food only through the surface. The middle of a deep or big pot is far from the surface, so it stays warm for many hours.
explanations.description: Heat is the jiggling of the tiny particles in a thing. Hot food cools when its particles pass their jiggling on to the air and the vessel. That can happen only at the surface. Heat from the middle must first travel to the surface, grain by grain. Thick food such as rice, upma or thick dal cannot flow, so this is slow. When food is spread thin, every part is near the surface. In a heap, the middle is far away. Size makes this worse. In a pot twice as wide, the heat has twice as far to go. There is also far more food for each bit of surface. Thick food in a pot twice as wide takes about four times as long to cool. So the middle of a wedding pot stays in the danger zone all night.
examples: Hot kanji poured on to a wide plate is cool enough for a baby in a minute or two.
A full pressure cooker of rice is still warm in the middle two hours later.
Cooks who make food for hundreds divide it into shallow trays to cool.
explanations.art: A cut-away drawing of a deep pot of rice with the middle coloured red and the edges blue, beside a flat tray of rice coloured blue all over.

explanations.concept: Cooling, storing and reheating cooked food
explanations.definition: Cool cooked food fast in shallow vessels and chill it within two hours. Reheat it until it steams all the way through.
explanations.description: Five habits follow from the science. First, cook only a little more than the family will eat. Second, put leftovers into shallow vessels, with the food no deeper than about three finger-widths. Third, get them into the fridge within two hours of cooking. A vessel standing in a tray of cold water cools faster still. Fourth, reheat only the amount you will eat. Heat it until it bubbles or steams in the middle, and stir, because the middle heats last too. Fifth, reheat leftovers only once, and eat fridge leftovers within about two days. Rice needs the most care. Spores of the bacterium Bacillus cereus survive cooking. In warm rice they wake, multiply and make a toxin that reheating does not destroy.
examples: Leftover rice spread in a flat steel box cools faster than rice left in the cooker.
A big vessel of hot sambar put straight into the fridge is still warm in the middle hours later.
Soup from the fridge is safe to serve when it bubbles all over, and the middle is hot too.
explanations.art: A deep cooker of rice with an arrow pointing to three flat steel boxes of rice with lids beside a fridge.

explanations.definition: Each food keeps longest in the place that blocks the way it is most likely to be lost.
explanations.description: Dry foods such as rice, dal, atta, rava, sugar and salt are lost to damp and pests. Keep them dry and airtight, away from the stove and the sink. Potatoes, onions and garlic are alive. Keep them cool, dark and airy, in a basket and never in a closed plastic bag. Light turns a potato green, and the green part holds a bitter poison called solanine. A very cold fridge turns some of a potato's starch to sugar. Bananas turn black in the fridge. Most other fruit and vegetables keep longer in the fridge, loosely wrapped so they do not dry. Milk, curd, eggs, cooked food, cut fruit, fish and meat are perishable and belong in the fridge. Oils and ghee keep best closed, cool and dark, because air and light turn them rancid. Bread grows mould more slowly in the fridge, though it turns stale faster there.
examples: Atta: an airtight steel dabba, because damp atta grows mould and draws beetles.
Potatoes: a dark, airy basket, because light turns them green.
Cooked dal: a shallow covered vessel in the fridge, because bacteria multiply in warm dal.
Cooking oil: a closed bottle away from the stove, because warmth and light turn oil rancid.
explanations.art: A kitchen drawn in cross-section with a steel dabba on a dry shelf, a basket of potatoes in a dark corner, a fridge with milk and covered bowls, and an oil bottle in a closed cupboard.

explanations.concept: Keeping grain and dal for a year
explanations.definition: Grain keeps for a year or more if it is dry enough, sealed from damp air and protected from insects.
explanations.description: Rice, wheat and dal are harvested once or twice a year and eaten every day. So someone must store them for months. Two enemies wait. The first is damp. Grain with more than about 14 parts of water in 100 lets moulds grow, though it looks dry. Some of these moulds make aflatoxin. So farmers dry grain in the sun before storing it, and families sun their rice and dal after the monsoon. The second enemy is insects. A rice weevil lays her eggs inside the grains. Families add dried neem leaves or dried chillies, which keep some insects away. A truly airtight container works better. The insects and the grain use up the oxygen inside it, and the insects stop feeding and die. Farmers now use sealed three-layer bags that work this way, with no chemical added.
examples: Rice spread on a terrace in the October sun before it goes back into the bin.
A tall clay or steel grain bin with a tight lid, in a village home in Tamil Nadu or Bihar.
A sealed bag of cowpeas in which the weevils stopped feeding within days.
explanations.art: A woman spreading rice on a cloth on a sunny terrace, with a tall steel grain bin with a tight lid standing in the doorway behind her.

explanations.concept: Pasteurised milk, UHT milk, tins and the cold chain
explanations.definition: Heat kills microbes in food, and a sealed pack or an unbroken line of cold keeps new growth away.
explanations.description: Pouch milk is pasteurised. It is heated to 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds, which kills the microbes that cause disease. Some harmless microbes and spores survive, so the pouch must stay cold from the dairy to your kitchen. That line of cold places is called a cold chain. An American chemist, Mary Engle Pennington, worked out many of its rules after 1905. She rode in railway wagons to measure how cold the food stayed. Carton milk is treated by UHT, which is heating to about 140 degrees for a few seconds. This kills the spores too, and the carton is filled without letting any microbe in. So it keeps for months on a shelf. A tin of food is heated after it is sealed. A tin or packet that has swollen holds gas made by living microbes. Never open or taste its food.
examples: India's milk cold chain begins at a village cooler. There the milk is chilled to 4 degrees Celsius within hours of milking.
An opened UHT carton is like pouch milk: keep it in the fridge and finish it in two days.
Ice cream that has melted and frozen again has ice crystals in it, a sign that the cold chain broke.
explanations.art: A woman in a village pouring a can of milk into a steel cooling tank, with an insulated milk tanker waiting outside.

explanations.definition: Extra care is needed for vulnerable people, for perishable foods and in hot or damp weather. It is also needed when food is cooked in large amounts or carried far.
explanations.description: Some people fall ill from fewer microbes than others. A baby has less acid in their stomach, and a small body loses water fast. A pregnant woman's defences are turned down a little, and a bacterium called Listeria can reach the baby inside her. Listeria is unusual because they can multiply slowly in a fridge. Old people and ill people also have weaker defences. For all of them, cook food fully and serve it fresh and hot. Avoid raw sprouts, raw milk and soft-boiled eggs. A baby under one year must not have honey. Honey can hold spores of a bacterium that grow in a baby's gut. Some foods need care for everyone: cooked rice, dal, milk sweets, cut fruit, eggs, fish and meat. Some days need care: the hot weeks of summer and the damp weeks of the monsoon. And some situations need care: feasts, lunch boxes, journeys and power cuts.
examples: A lunch box packed at 7 and eaten at 1 has spent six hours in the danger zone.
A fridge with its door kept shut stays cold for about four hours in a power cut.
For a feast, food cooked the night before is the usual cause of trouble.
explanations.art: A family table with a baby, a pregnant woman, a grandmother and a child, and a plate of hot idlis being served.

explanations.concept: Hot food: straight into the fridge, or cool it first?
explanations.definition: Cooks and food safety agencies agree that cooked food must be chilled within two hours. They disagree about whether it must cool on the counter first.
explanations.description: Many families wait until food reaches room temperature before it goes in the fridge. Food safety agencies now say that waiting is the bigger risk. The answer depends on the amount of food and on the fridge.
examples: A katori of warm dal hardly changes the temperature of a fridge.
A five-litre pot of hot sambar can warm everything on its shelf for hours.

perspectives.explanation: Hot food warms the fridge and the milk and curd beside it, and steam turns to drops and frost. The fridge then works harder and uses more electricity. So food should cool on the counter first.

perspectives.who: Food safety agencies, such as the Food Safety and Inspection Service of the United States
perspectives.explanation: Food left to cool on a counter can spend many hours in the danger zone. Small amounts in shallow vessels can go into the fridge while still warm. A modern fridge can remove that heat.
Both are right about a different pot. A big pot must never go in whole, because its middle stays warm in any fridge. Divide it, stand the trays in cold water for half an hour, and then chill them.

explanations.art: A woman holding a pot of steaming dal in front of an open fridge, looking at a clock on the wall.

agreed.text: Microbes cause most spoilage of moist food.
agreed.evidence: Food that is heated in a sealed tin stays good for years, because no living microbe is inside. The same food spoils within days once the tin is opened.

agreed.text: Bacteria multiply fastest in warm food, and slowly or not at all in a cold fridge.
agreed.evidence: In 1982 David Ratkowsky and his team in Tasmania measured how fast many kinds of bacteria grew at different temperatures. Growth fell steadily as the temperature fell, and stopped for most kinds near fridge temperature.

agreed.text: Large amounts of food that cool slowly cause many outbreaks of food poisoning.
agreed.evidence: Health officers who trace outbreaks at feasts and canteens often find food that was cooked hours ahead in big vessels. In laboratory tests, spores of the bacterium Clostridium perfringens multiplied in cooked food that was cooled slowly. They did not multiply in food that was cooled fast.

agreed.text: Moulds on damp grain and nuts can make poisons that cooking does not destroy.
agreed.evidence: In 1960 about 100,000 young turkeys in England died after eating mouldy groundnut meal. In 1974 mouldy maize poisoned people in about 200 villages of Gujarat and Rajasthan. Rain had wet the maize.

agreed.text: Babies under one year should not be given honey.
agreed.evidence: In 1979 Stephen Arnon and his team in California studied babies with an illness called infant botulism. Many of the ill babies had been fed honey. The team found the spores of the bacterium in samples of that honey.

agreed.text: Fresh fruit and vegetables are still alive after they are picked.
agreed.evidence: They go on taking in oxygen and giving out carbon dioxide and water. In 2013 Janet Braam's team in Texas studied cabbages bought from a shop. The cabbages still kept a daily rhythm of day and night.

challenging.who: A warning that is often passed around.
challenging.for: People have fallen ill after eating reheated rice. Spores of Bacillus cereus survive cooking, and the toxin survives reheating.
challenging.against: The harm is done before the reheating, while the rice sits warm for hours. Rice that was cooled fast, chilled within an hour or two and reheated once until steaming is safe.
challenging.context: This is a common warning about leftover rice, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.claim: Rice left overnight in water is unsafe, because it breaks the two-hour rule.
challenging.for: Cooked rice at room temperature for twelve hours is exactly what the two-hour rule forbids. Bacillus cereus spores are common on rice.
challenging.against: Millions of people eat this soaked rice every summer. It is called pazhaya sadam in Tamil Nadu, pakhala in Odisha and panta bhat in Bengal. The water turns sour as lactic acid bacteria grow, and sourness holds back many harmful bacteria. Few careful studies have measured how safe it is.
challenging.context: This is a real disagreement between an old food habit and a modern safety rule.

challenging.claim: Freezing kills microbes, so frozen food is safe for ever.
challenging.for: Frozen food does not spoil, even after months.
challenging.against: Freezing stops microbes from multiplying, but most of them stay alive. They start again when the food thaws. So thawed food is as perishable as fresh food.
challenging.context: This is a common idea about freezers, with the evidence for it and against it.

challenging.claim: Eggs must always be kept in the fridge.
challenging.who: Shops and health agencies in some countries, such as the United States.
challenging.for: Cold slows any bacteria on or in the egg, and eggs keep several weeks longer in a fridge.
challenging.against: In much of Europe eggs are sold from open shelves. An unwashed shell has a natural coat that keeps bacteria out. In an Indian summer, a fridge is the safer place.
challenging.context: This is a question on which countries follow different rules.

challenging.claim: One rotten fruit spoils the whole basket.
challenging.who: An old saying in many languages.
challenging.for: Mould from one fruit makes millions of spores, and juice from a rotting fruit wets the fruit beside it. Ripe fruit also gives off a gas that ripens the others.
challenging.against: The fruit must touch or share still air for this to happen. Sorting the basket each day stops it.
challenging.context: This is an old saying about stored fruit. Here is what science says about it.

challenging.claim: If food was boiled and then covered, nothing can grow in it.
challenging.for: Boiling kills most bacteria, and a lid keeps flies and dust out.
challenging.against: The spores of some bacteria survive boiling. They wake when the food cools to a warm temperature, and a lid does not stop them. Only time and temperature do.
challenging.context: This is a common belief in kitchens, with the evidence for it and against it.

big_questions.q: A covered pot of dal looks the same at night and the next morning. What can change in food without leaving any sign?
big_questions.hint: Think of the doubling table. Which of your senses could count bacteria?

big_questions.q: When a safety rule works, nobody falls ill and nothing happens. How can anyone know that the rule worked?
big_questions.hint: Compare many kitchens that follow the rule with many that do not.

big_questions.q: A cook throws away 30 kilograms of dal that might have been safe. Is that waste, or is it care?
big_questions.hint: Who pays if she is wrong one way? Who pays if she is wrong the other way?

big_questions.q: Milk spoils in turns, as each microbe changes it for the next. Is spoiling an ending, or a line of many lives?
big_questions.hint: A forest also arrives in turns: grass, then bushes, then trees.

big_questions.q: The two-hour rule is the same for a baby and for a wrestler. Should a rule be written for the strongest person, or for the weakest?
big_questions.hint: Who sits at a wedding lunch? Who is harmed if the rule is too loose?

big_questions.q: A potato in the basket is alive, and a cooked potato is not. When exactly did the potato stop being alive?
big_questions.hint: Was it the peeling, the cutting or the heat? Could any piece still have grown?

story.title: The Middle of the Pot
story.note: Poongodi, Mallika, Paatti, Kanmani and the two weddings are made up. These facts are real. Kumbakonam, Thirunageswaram and Swamimalai are towns in Thanjavur district in Tamil Nadu. Wedding cooks there feed hundreds of guests from very large vessels. A big vessel of thick cooked food stays warm in the middle for many hours. The spores of some bacteria survive boiling and multiply in food that stays warm, without changing its look or smell. Cooks who feed large numbers cool food in shallow trays for this reason.
text: Poongodi was eleven, and this was her first wedding as a worker.

Her aunt Mallika cooked for weddings in and around Kumbakonam. Tomorrow six hundred guests would sit down to lunch on banana leaves. Tonight, in the shed behind the wedding hall, three wood fires burned under vessels big enough to bathe in.
Poongodi had three jobs. She peeled garlic. She carried water. And she minded Kanmani, her aunt's baby, who slept in a cloth cradle tied to a beam.
At nine o'clock Kanmani woke and howled. Her ragi kanji had come straight off the fire. Poongodi blew on a spoonful and touched it to her lip. It was far too hot. Kanmani howled louder.

So Poongodi did what Paatti always did at home. She poured the kanji out of the tumbler on to a wide steel plate. She tilted the plate this way and that, until the kanji lay as thin as a dosa. She counted slowly to sixty. Then she touched it with her little finger. It was only warm. Kanmani ate every spoonful and went back to sleep with ragi on her chin.
By then the dal was done. Thirty kilos of toor dal had boiled for an hour in the biggest vessel, for tomorrow's sambar.

"Boil the dal tonight and we save two hours in the morning," Mallika said. Two women lifted the lid, which was as wide as an open umbrella, and set it on the vessel. Everyone washed. Then they lay down on mats in the hall, and one by one they slept.
Poongodi could not sleep. The hall smelled of jasmine and the fans were loud. Some time after three she got up for a drink of water. The shed was dark. The fires were grey ash.
She passed the dal vessel and laid her palm on its side, the way you pat a cow in the dark. Near the top the metal was cool. Lower down it was warm.
That was strange. The fire had been out for six hours.

She lifted the edge of the lid and took the long ladle. She pushed it down into the very middle of the dal and brought it up, and held her finger over it. The dal from the middle was as warm as bath water.
Poongodi stood there with the ladle. The baby's kanji had cooled while she counted to sixty. This dal had been cooling for six hours, and its middle was still warm. It would be warm at sunrise.
She thought of what Paatti said about milk, every summer. Hot is safe and cold is safe. Warm is where it turns.
She did not want to wake her aunt. Mallika had been on her feet since four the morning before. And who was Poongodi? She was the girl who peeled the garlic. She woke her all the same.
Mallika came with her hair loose and her eyes half shut. She bent over the vessel and smelled the dal. She held the lamp close and looked at it.
"It boiled for an hour," she said. "It was covered. It smells sweet. I have done it this way for twenty years."
"It has been warm all night, Athai. It is still warm in the middle. Paatti says warm is where it turns."
"Your Paatti says that about milk."
"Is dal so different?"

Mallika did not answer. Rain had begun on the tin roof. She put her own palm on the vessel, high and then low. She took the ladle and brought up dal from the middle, and felt it, and stood still for a long time.
"Thirunageswaram," she said at last, not to Poongodi. "Four years ago. Forty people were ill after a lunch of mine, and I never knew which dish. I blamed the well."
She looked at the vessel. "Thirty kilos. That is four thousand rupees. And nobody can tell me that it has turned."
"Nobody can tell you that it has not," Poongodi said, and was frightened by her own mouth.

Mallika woke the women at four. The old dal went into the pit behind the hall, where the used banana leaves would go. New dal went on two fires in two smaller vessels, and it was soft before six. The sambar was late by nobody's clock but Mallika's.
Six hundred people ate. They praised the sambar and asked for more of it. Nobody fell ill. Nobody knew there had been a first dal.
Poongodi ate last, sitting on an upturned bucket. Would anyone have fallen ill? She would never find out. The pit had the dal, and the pit was not going to tell her.
A month later there was a wedding in Swamimalai. Poongodi came into the cooking shed at night with her basket of garlic, and stopped.

The big vessel stood empty. The dal for the morning lay in twelve wide trays, two fingers deep. The trays stood in a stone trough of well water, each under a square of thin cloth. A woman was moving along the row with a palm-leaf fan.
Mallika did not look up from the fire.
"Like your kanji," she said. "Now go and peel the garlic."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Poongodi cooled the baby's kanji in a minute by spreading it thin on a plate. The dal in the huge vessel was still warm in the middle after six hours. Heat leaves food only at the surface. So a big, deep pot holds its middle in the warm range for a whole night. That warm range is where surviving spores multiply, and nothing in the look or smell shows it. Mallika's twelve shallow trays at the end are the baby's plate again, made large.
ask: The kanji cooled in a minute, and the dal was still warm after six hours. What was different about them?
The dal looked and smelled fine. Why could Mallika not find out whether it was safe?
Nobody fell ill at the wedding. Does that show that Poongodi was right? What would you need to know?
At the second wedding the dal lay in twelve trays in water. Why does that work better than one big vessel?
art: A cooking shed at night behind a wedding hall, with three wood fires under very large vessels and a baby asleep in a cloth cradle tied to a beam.
A girl of eleven tilting a wide steel plate so that brown ragi kanji spreads thin across the plate, while a baby reaches out from a cradle.
A girl alone in a dark shed laying her palm on the side of a vessel taller than her waist, with grey ash under the vessel.
A tired woman with loose hair holding a lamp over an open vessel of yellow dal, with a girl beside her holding a long ladle.
Twelve wide trays of dal under thin cloths standing in a stone trough of water, with a woman fanning them and a girl in the doorway with a basket of garlic.

games.title: Serve, Change or Stop? A game about extra care
games.context: This is a card game about when food needs extra care. Each card describes a food, the way it was kept and the person who will eat it. You decide whether to serve it, change something first, or stop.

printables.title: 20 situation cards, with the answer on the back

items.f: Idlis steamed ten minutes ago, for a baby of 8 months.
items.b: SERVE. Fresh, steaming food has had no time in the danger zone. Mash the idli and leave out the chilli.

items.f: Honey spread on a dosa, for a baby of 10 months.
items.b: STOP. No honey before the first birthday. Honey can hold spores that grow in a baby's gut.

items.f: Raw sprouted moong salad, for a pregnant aunt.
items.b: CHANGE. Steam or boil the sprouts first. Sprouting is warm and wet, so bacteria multiply on sprouts too.

items.f: Yesterday's rice, chilled within an hour of cooking, for a healthy child of ten.
items.b: CHANGE. Reheat only what you will eat, until it steams in the middle. Reheat it once.

items.f: Rice left in the cooker on the counter since last night, in May.
items.b: STOP. The rice was warm for twelve hours. Reheating does not destroy the toxin that Bacillus cereus makes.

items.f: Watermelon from a roadside cart, cut hours ago, for a grandmother of 80.
items.b: STOP. Cut fruit is wet and not sour, so bacteria multiply on it. Buy a whole fruit and cut it at home.

items.f: Milk straight from a dairy farm, not yet boiled, for the family.
items.b: CHANGE. Boil it first. Raw milk can carry bacteria from the cow or the buffalo.

items.f: A soft-boiled egg with a runny yolk, for a cousin who is recovering from typhoid.
items.b: CHANGE. Boil the egg until the yolk is firm. A body that has just been ill has weaker defences.

items.f: Curd rice made at 7 in the morning, eaten from a lunch box at 1.
items.b: SERVE. Curd is sour, and sourness holds back most harmful bacteria. On a very hot day, pack it with a cold pack.

items.f: A tin of food with a swollen lid.
items.b: STOP. The gas inside was made by living microbes. Do not open the tin and do not taste the food.

items.f: Sambar for 300 guests, cooked last night and left in the big vessel.
items.b: STOP. The middle of a big vessel stays warm all night. Boiling it again may not remove every toxin.

items.f: Dal that was cooled in a flat box, chilled within an hour, and is two days old.
items.b: CHANGE. Reheat it until it bubbles, and stir the middle. Finish it today.

items.f: Milk from a fridge after a power cut of 3 hours. The door stayed shut.
items.b: SERVE. A closed fridge stays cold for about four hours. Boil the milk before use, as usual.

items.f: Fish curry from a fridge after a power cut of 10 hours in summer.
items.b: STOP. After about four hours the fridge warms into the danger zone. Fish curry is perishable.

items.f: Groundnuts from an old packet. Some are shrivelled, and one has grey-green mould.
items.b: STOP. Throw the packet away. The mould may have made aflatoxin, which roasting does not destroy.

items.f: A potato with a small green patch and two sprouts.
items.b: CHANGE. Cut away the green part and the sprouts, with a thick margin. If most of the potato is green, throw it away.

items.f: Pani puri from a street stall in the monsoon, for a pregnant aunt.
items.b: STOP. The water is not boiled, and dirty water spreads most illness in the monsoon. Make pani puri at home with boiled water.

items.f: Chapatis and dry roasted potato, packed for a train journey of 6 hours.
items.b: SERVE. Dry food has little free water, so bacteria multiply slowly on it.

items.f: A loaf of bread with one small spot of green mould on one slice.
items.b: STOP. In soft food the hyphae spread far beyond the spot you see. Throw the loaf away in a closed bag.

items.f: Fresh fish carried home for one hour in May with no ice.
items.b: CHANGE. Cook the fish at once, and cook it fully. Next time, carry ice in the bag.

rules: Shuffle the 20 cards and put them in a pile with the situations facing up.
One player is the reader for the round. The reader reads the top card aloud and does not turn it over.
The other players think for ten seconds. On the word 'go', each player holds up fingers: one for SERVE, two for CHANGE, three for STOP.
A player who shows two fingers must say what they would change. A player who shows three must say why.
The reader turns the card over and reads the answer. A right call scores 1 point. The right change or reason scores 1 more.
The next player becomes the reader. Play until all 20 cards are used. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone? Sort the 20 cards into three piles: SERVE, CHANGE and STOP. Then check the backs. Play again later and try to beat your score.

setup.art: Twenty paper cards in a pile on a table, with three children sitting around the pile.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. Put them in a pile with the situations facing up.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while two others hold up one, two or three fingers.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. The others hold up one finger for serve, two for change, three for stop.

setup.art: A child turning a card over to read the answer on the back.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over and read the answer. Give the points.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards. Read the rules together. Practise the three finger signs once.
flow.say: Each card tells you a food, how it was kept and who will eat it. One finger means serve. Two fingers mean change something first. Three fingers mean stop.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. One finger is serve. Two is change. Three is stop.
flow.context: This is the first step of Serve, Change or Stop. You learn the three signs.

flow.do: Play through the pile. After each answer, ask the player which clue on the card decided it.
flow.say: Read the card and wait ten seconds. Then say go. After the answer, tell us which clue decided it: the food, the hours, the warmth or the person.
flow.kid: Hold up your fingers on go. Say what you would change, or why you stop.

ask.q: Which clue decided this card: the food, the hours, the warmth or the person?
good: The hours: it was warm for too long.
The person: a baby needs more care.
The food: it is wet and not sour.
The warmth: the fridge had warmed up.

flow.parent: Many cards turn on one clue. A baby and honey, a swollen tin and mould on soft food are always stop. Leftovers that were chilled fast are change: reheat until steaming.
flow.context: In this step of Serve, Change or Stop you play all 20 cards. You name the clue that decides each one.

flow.do: Count the points. Lay out all the STOP cards together and ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the stop cards. Could you have seen or smelled the problem in every one of them? Which ones give no sign at all?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which stop cards give no sign you can see or smell?

check.q: Rice was kept warm for twelve hours and then reheated until it steamed. Why is it still a STOP?
options: The toxin stays after heating
Reheated rice has no taste
Steam makes rice wet
check.why: Bacillus cereus makes a toxin while the rice sits warm, and heat does not destroy that toxin. If you chose another answer, remember that the harm is done in the warm hours, before the reheating.

flow.context: This is the last step of Serve, Change or Stop. You look at the cards where the food must not be served.

games.title: The Keep Line: which food keeps longer?
games.context: This is a card game about shelf life. Each card names a food and the place where it is kept. You place the cards in a line. The food that keeps for the shortest time goes at one end, and the longest at the other.

printables.title: 20 food cards, with the keeping time and the reason on the back

items.f: Cooked dal on the kitchen counter in summer
items.b: About 2 hours. Warm, wet food that is not sour is where bacteria multiply fastest.

items.f: Boiled milk, covered, on the counter in summer
items.b: About 6 hours. Boiling kills most microbes, but spores survive and the milk stays warm.

items.f: Spinach leaves on the counter in summer
items.b: About 12 hours. The leaves are alive and lose water fast, so they wilt and turn yellow.

items.f: Fresh fish in the fridge
items.b: About 1 day. Some bacteria on sea fish can multiply even in the cold.

items.f: An opened pouch of milk in the fridge
items.b: About 2 days. Pasteurising leaves some microbes alive, and cold only slows them.

items.f: Ripe bananas on the counter
items.b: About 3 days. The fruit is alive and goes on ripening until the skin is black.

items.f: A packet of bread on the shelf
items.b: About 5 days. Bread is too dry for most bacteria, so moulds spoil it slowly.

items.f: Home-made curd in the fridge
items.b: About 1 week. Curd is sour, which holds back most bacteria, but yeasts and moulds grow in time.

items.f: Ripe tomatoes in the fridge
items.b: About 2 weeks. Cold slows the tomato's own ripening and the moulds on the skin.

items.f: Potatoes in a cool, dark, airy basket
items.b: About 3 weeks in a warm kitchen. After that they sprout, because they are alive.

items.f: Eggs in the fridge
items.b: About 5 weeks. The shell and the cold keep most bacteria out.

items.f: Onions in a dry, airy basket
items.b: About 2 months. Their dry outer skins keep water in and microbes out.

items.f: Whole wheat atta in an airtight dabba
items.b: About 3 months. The little oil in the wheat germ slowly turns rancid.

items.f: An unopened carton of UHT milk on the shelf
items.b: About 6 months. The heating killed even the spores, and the carton lets no microbe in.

items.f: Ghee in a closed jar on the shelf
items.b: About 9 months. Ghee has almost no water, so microbes cannot grow. Air slowly turns it rancid.

items.f: Mango pickle under a layer of oil
items.b: About 1 year. Salt, sourness and the oil cover each hold microbes back.

items.f: White rice in a dry, airtight bin
items.b: About 2 years. Dry grain gives microbes no free water, and the bin keeps pests out.

items.f: An unopened tin of beans
items.b: About 3 years. The tin was heated after sealing, so nothing alive is inside.

items.f: Honey in a closed jar
items.b: More than 10 years. The sugar holds the water so tightly that microbes cannot use it.

items.f: Dry salt in a jar
items.b: For ever. Salt is a mineral, and no microbe can live on dry salt.

rules: Shuffle the 20 cards with the food side up. Deal 4 cards to each player, food side up on the table. Nobody looks at the backs.
Put one card from the pile in the middle and turn it over. This card starts the Keep Line.
On your turn, choose one of your cards. Put it in the line where you think it belongs: to the left if it keeps for a shorter time, to the right if longer.
Turn your card over. If it is in the right place, it stays. If it is wrong, move it to its right place and take a new card from the pile.
Read the reason on the back aloud each time.
The first player with no cards left wins. If the pile runs out, the player with the fewest cards wins.
Playing alone? Lay all 20 cards in one line by your best guess. Then turn them over, and count how many are out of order.
The times are careful rules of thumb for a warm Indian kitchen at about 30 degrees Celsius.

setup.art: Paper cards with food names laid face up in front of two players, and one card turned over in the middle of the table.
setup.caption: 1. Deal 4 cards each, food side up. Turn one card over in the middle to start the line.

setup.art: A child sliding a card into a gap between two cards in a row on the table.
setup.caption: 2. Put a card where you think it belongs: shorter time to the left, longer time to the right.

setup.art: A row of turned-over cards reading from 2 hours on the left to for ever on the right.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to check. A wrong card moves to its right place, and you take a new card.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and read the rules. Before you deal, ask which food in the kitchen your child thinks keeps longest, and why.
flow.say: Which food in our kitchen do you think keeps the longest? Which spoils the fastest? What makes you think so?
flow.kid: Which food keeps longest? Which spoils fastest? Say why you think so.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Keep Line. You guess which foods keep longest before you play.

flow.do: Play until one player has no cards. Each time a card is turned, the player reads the reason aloud.
flow.say: Place your card, then turn it over and read the reason. Listen for what protects each food: dryness, sourness, salt, sugar, cold or a seal.
flow.kid: Place a card in the line. Turn it over. Read the reason aloud.
flow.parent: Children often place fridge foods too far to the right. Cold only slows microbes. Dry, sealed and very sweet foods keep far longer than chilled ones.
flow.context: In this step of the Keep Line you place the food cards in order of how long they keep.

flow.do: Look at the finished line together. Ask the questions below.
flow.say: Look at the left end and the right end of the line. What are the foods on the left like? What are the foods on the right like?
flow.kid: Look at both ends of the line. How are the two ends different?

ask.q: What do the foods at the left end have in common?
good: They are wet.
They are not sour, salty or very sweet.
They are warm.
Some are still alive, like the leaves.

ask.q: What do the foods at the right end have in common?
good: They are dry.
They are sealed.
They are full of salt or sugar.
Microbes cannot get water from them.

check.q: Curd in the fridge keeps a week. Dry rice in a bin keeps two years. What does that show?
options: Dryness protects food longer than cold does
Cold kills more microbes than dryness
Rice has no microbes on it
check.why: Cold only slows microbes down. Without free water they cannot grow at all. If you chose 'cold kills', remember that most microbes in a fridge stay alive.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Keep Line. You compare the foods at the two ends of the line.

experiments.title: Deep or Shallow: how long does the middle of hot rice stay hot?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put the same hot rice in a deep bowl and on a wide plate. You time how long each stays hotter than 43 degrees Celsius. It shows why a big pot of cooked food stays in the danger zone for hours.
experiments.question: The same hot rice is heaped in a deep bowl and spread thin on a plate. How many minutes does each take to fall below 43 degrees Celsius? Is the edge of the heap as hot as the middle?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which rice will cool first, and by how many minutes? Will the edge of the bowl and the middle of the bowl cool together? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use rice from one pot, cooked at the same time. Put the same amount, 2 cups, in the bowl and on the plate. Keep both in the same place, away from the fan and the window. Use the same thermometer and the same waiting time for each reading. Only one thing changes: the shape of the rice.

materials.item: freshly cooked hot rice, 4 cups (from about 1 and a half cups of raw rice)
a deep steel bowl that holds 2 cups when full
a wide steel plate with a rim
a cup for measuring the rice
a digital fever thermometer, washed with soap. Never use a glass thermometer
a clock or a phone timer
a spoon, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up serves the hot rice and makes every reading in the first ten minutes. Steam from the middle of the heap can scald. Never use a glass thermometer, because it can break in hot food. Rice straight from the cooker can also harm a fever thermometer, so keep to the times in the steps. Wash the thermometer tip with soap before and after.

schedule.what: Heap hot rice in a bowl and spread the same amount on a plate. Take readings for an hour, and work out what the times show.

experiments.record: Draw a table with a row for 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 minutes. In each box write 'too hot', HI, or the number the thermometer shows. Circle the first number in each column.

setup.art: A deep steel bowl packed full of steaming rice next to a wide steel plate with rice spread in a thin, even layer.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up presses 2 cups of hot rice into a deep bowl and spreads 2 cups thin on a plate.

setup.art: A hand pushing the tip of a digital thermometer into the thin layer of rice on the plate, with the screen showing the letters HI.
setup.caption: 2. Push the thermometer tip into the rice. HI means hotter than about 43 degrees Celsius.

setup.art: A child writing in a table in a notebook, with a clock beside the bowl and the plate.
setup.caption: 3. Measure the plate from 5 minutes, the edge of the bowl from 20 minutes and the middle from 40 minutes.

setup.art: A spoon opening the middle of the heap of rice in the bowl, with a child holding one hand above the opening and the other hand above the plate of rice.
setup.caption: 4. After an hour, open the middle of the heap with a spoon. Hold a hand above the heap, and then above the plate.

flow.do: Check the thermometer in a cup of hot tap water. Most digital fever thermometers show HI or H above about 43 degrees Celsius. Then ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: I will put the same hot rice in this bowl and on this plate. Which will cool first, and by how many minutes? Will the edge of the bowl cool with the middle? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Hot rice goes in a bowl and on a plate. Which cools first? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Where does the heat of the rice go when the rice cools?
good: Into the air.
Into the plate and the table.
It leaves from the outside of the rice.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. If your thermometer shows a number in hot tap water, read its leaflet for the highest temperature it can show. No thermometer at home? Use the steam test in the note of step 3.
flow.context: This is the first step of Deep or Shallow. You guess how fast heaped rice and spread rice will cool.

flow.do: 1. Take the rice straight from the cooker. 2. Press 2 cups into the deep bowl, up to the top. 3. Spread 2 cups on the plate, about as thick as your finger. 4. Start the clock.
flow.say: I am filling the bowl to the top and pressing the rice down. Now I am spreading the same amount on the plate, as thick as a finger. The clock starts now.
flow.kid: A grown-up fills the bowl and spreads the plate. Start the clock.
flow.parent: Work fast, so that both lots start equally hot. Keep them side by side, away from a fan.
flow.context: In this step of Deep or Shallow a grown-up puts hot rice in a bowl and on a plate.

flow.do: At 5, 10, 15 and 20 minutes, push the tip 1 centimetre into the plate rice. Write HI or the number. The bowl is still too hot for a fever thermometer, so write 'too hot'. At 20 minutes, take the first reading at the edge of the bowl, 3 centimetres deep.
flow.say: We measure the plate every five minutes. The bowl is too hot for this thermometer at first, so we write 'too hot'. At twenty minutes we measure the edge of the bowl. Wait for the beep each time.
flow.kid: Measure the plate every five minutes. At twenty minutes, measure the edge of the bowl.

check.q: In Deep or Shallow, why must the bowl and the plate hold the same amount of rice?
options: So that only the shape is different
So that nobody gets more rice
So that the thermometer fits
check.why: A fair test changes one thing. Here that one thing is the shape of the rice. If the amounts were different too, you could not tell which one caused the result.

flow.parent: The plate rice usually shows a number within 10 to 15 minutes. A kitchen thermometer with a metal probe can measure all three places from the start. The steam test, if you have no thermometer: at 20, 40 and 60 minutes, open each place a little with a spoon and look for steam. Then a grown-up touches the rice with the back of a finger. Write 'steam', 'hot', 'warm' or 'cool'. Between readings, you can begin the activity Three Clocks.
flow.context: In this step of Deep or Shallow you take readings on the plate every five minutes. At 20 minutes you also measure the edge of the bowl.

flow.do: Take readings at 30, 40, 50 and 60 minutes. Measure the plate and the edge of the bowl each time. From 40 minutes, also push the tip into the middle of the bowl. Stop a column when it has shown a number twice.
flow.say: Keep going every ten minutes. From forty minutes we can measure the middle of the bowl too. Which place is still at HI? How much longer do you think it will take?
flow.kid: Take readings every ten minutes. From forty minutes, measure the middle too.
flow.parent: A thermometer shows LO when the rice falls below about 32 degrees Celsius. If the middle of the bowl is still at HI after 60 minutes, write 'more than 60'. That is a good result.
flow.context: In this step of Deep or Shallow you go on taking readings until an hour has passed.

flow.do: At 60 minutes, your child opens the middle of the heap with a spoon. They hold one hand a little above the opening, and then above the plate rice. Circle the first number in each column of the table.
flow.say: Open the middle of the heap with the spoon. Hold your hand just above it. Now hold your hand above the plate. What do you feel? Circle the first number in each column.
flow.kid: Open the middle with a spoon. Hold a hand above it. Now try the plate.
flow.parent: The test rice is still safe, because one hour is inside the two-hour rule. Eat it now, or put it out for the crows. Do not put it back in the family pot, because it has been handled.
flow.context: In this step of Deep or Shallow you open the heap after an hour and compare it with the plate.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Look at your three columns. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Why was the middle of the bowl the last place to cool?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: Why did the middle of the bowl stay hot the longest?
good: The heat had to travel through all the rice around it.
The middle is far from the air.
Heat only leaves from the outside.

ask.q: A wedding pot is five times as wide as your bowl. What happens in its middle overnight?
good: It stays warm for many hours.
It stays in the danger zone all night.
Microbes can multiply in it.

flow.parent: The reason: heat leaves food only through its surface. On the plate, every grain is near the surface. In the bowl, heat from the middle must pass from grain to grain to reach the outside. That is slow. Bacteria multiply between about 5 and 60 degrees Celsius, and fastest between 20 and 45. So the middle of a deep pot spends the longest time at the temperatures bacteria like best. Thick food in a pot twice as wide takes about four times as long to cool.
flow.think: Why do many families cool a baby's kanji by pouring it on to a plate?
flow.context: This is the last step of Deep or Shallow. You say what your readings show about how hot food cools.

experiments.title: Three Sealed Bags: which microbes spoil which food?
experiments.context: In this six-day experiment you seal damp bread, wet rice, a lemon slice and dry toast in clear bags. You watch which bag changes first and what the change looks like. It shows that different microbes spoil different foods.
experiments.question: Damp bread, wet cooked rice, a slice of lemon and a piece of dry toast are sealed in clear bags. Which changes first? Do they all spoil in the same way?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which bag will change first, and which last? What will each food look like when it spoils: fuzzy, slimy, or something else? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use four bags of the same kind and size. Leave all four foods open on one plate for the same 30 minutes, so the same air reaches them. Keep the sealed bags side by side in the same warm, shaded place. Look at the same time each day. Only one thing changes: the food in the bag.
results_table: What I saw: slime, liquid, fuzz, colour or a puffed bag

materials.item: clear zip bags, or clear plastic boxes with lids
a slice of bread, or half a chapati
cooked rice, 2 tablespoons
a thick slice of lemon
a piece of bread toasted until hard and dry, or a dry rusk
water and a teaspoon
sticky tape and a marker pen
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera that can zoom

experiments.safety: Once the bags are sealed, never open them again. Do not smell or taste anything from them. On the last day, throw the sealed bags into the dustbin. A child who has asthma or a mould allergy watches, and a grown-up handles the bags. Wash your hands after touching the bags.

schedule.what: Guess, set out the four foods, and seal them in four labelled bags.
Look at each bag without opening it. Draw or write any change.
Look again. Use the magnifying glass on any spot.
Make the last record. Say what the bags show, and throw them away sealed.

experiments.record: Make a page for each day. Draw the four bags. Beside each write what you see: no change, wet, slimy, a coloured patch, fuzz, or a puffed bag. Note the day of the first change for each bag.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: White fuzz, then green and black dots
Slimy and watery, with yellow patches. The bag puffed a little
Hard and dry, as on day 1

setup.art: A plate with a slice of bread, a small heap of cooked rice, a thick slice of lemon and a piece of dry toast, with a teaspoon of water beside the plate.
setup.caption: 1. Put the four foods on a plate. Sprinkle half a teaspoon of water on the bread and a teaspoon on the rice.

setup.art: The same plate left on a kitchen counter with a clock showing half an hour later.
setup.caption: 2. Leave the plate open for 30 minutes, so that microbes from the air land on the foods.

setup.art: Four clear zip bags labelled A, B, C and D, each holding one food, sealed and taped shut.
setup.caption: 3. Seal each food in its own bag. Tape the seal. Label the bags A, B, C and D.

setup.art: A child looking through a magnifying glass at a fuzzy spot on bread inside a sealed clear bag.
setup.caption: 4. Look through the bags every day for six days. Never open them.

flow.do: Day 1. Ask for the guess and the reasons, and write them down. Sprinkle half a teaspoon of water on the bread and one teaspoon on the rice. Leave the four foods open for 30 minutes. Then seal each in a labelled bag and tape it shut. Keep the bags in a warm, shaded place.
flow.say: We will seal four foods in four bags. Which will change first? What will each look like when it spoils? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Four foods go in four bags. Which spoils first? What will it look like? Why?

ask.q: We add no microbes. Where will the microbes in the bags come from?
good: From the air.
They are already on the food.
From our hands and the plate.

flow.parent: Leave a little air in each bag, because moulds need air. Keep the bags out of direct sun, which would cook the food. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Three Sealed Bags. You guess, and seal four foods in four clear bags.

flow.do: Days 2 to 5. Look at each bag at the same time each day, without opening it. Hold the magnifying glass to any spot. Your child draws or writes what they see.
flow.say: Look closely through the bag. Is anything wet, shiny, coloured or fuzzy? Has the bag puffed up? Write down what you see, even if nothing has changed.
flow.kid: Look through each bag. Do you see slime, colour, fuzz or a puffed bag? Write it down.
flow.wait: Look once a day for the next four days

check.q: In Three Sealed Bags, why is one bag filled with dry toast?
options: To test a food with no free water
Because toast tastes better
To use up the old bread
check.why: The dry toast is the comparison. It shows whether the same microbes can spoil a food that has no free water. If you chose another answer, remember that a fair test needs something to compare with.

flow.parent: In warm weather the wet rice usually changes first, within one or two days. It turns shiny, slimy and watery, often with yellow, orange or pink patches. The bread grows fuzzy spots after three to five days. The lemon often shows nothing for a week. In winter, everything takes about twice as long.
flow.context: On days 2 to 5 of Three Sealed Bags you look at the four bags and record any change.

flow.do: Day 6. Make the last record. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below. Then throw the sealed bags into the dustbin.
flow.say: Look at your six days of records. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Why did the rice and the bread not spoil in the same way?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened.

ask.q: The rice turned slimy and the bread turned fuzzy. What does that tell you?
good: Different microbes grew on them.
Bacteria grew on the wet rice.
Moulds grew on the drier bread.

ask.q: Why did the lemon change last, or not at all?
good: Lemon is very sour.
Bacteria cannot grow in so much acid.
Only some moulds can, and they are slow.

flow.parent: The reason: bacteria multiply fastest, but they need plenty of free water and little acid. The wet rice suits them, and they make slime, liquid and gas. Bread is too dry for most bacteria, so slower moulds get the bread. A mould looks fuzzy because they grow as fine threads called hyphae. The coloured dots hold their spores. Lemon is too sour for almost all bacteria, so only a few slow moulds can use it. Dry toast gives no microbe enough water. If your lemon shows nothing by day 6, keep that bag sealed for another week and look again.
flow.think: Idli batter is wet and warm, yet it turns sour and safe. Which microbes got there first?
flow.context: This is the last day of Three Sealed Bags. You say what the four bags show about which microbes spoil which food.

experiments.title: Dry Enough? The salt jar test for stored rice
experiments.context: In this experiment you shake dry salt with rice in closed jars. If the rice is too damp to store, the salt takes up the damp and sticks. Farmers use this test before they store grain. The experiment has a wait of 45 minutes in the middle.
experiments.question: Rice from the dabba is dry. A second lot of rice has been wetted a little and now looks dry again. Can dry salt in a closed jar show which rice is too damp to store?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After the wetted rice looks dry again, will it behave like the dabba rice? What will the salt do in each jar? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use three jars of the same size, all completely dry. Put the same amount of rice, half a cup, and the same amount of salt, one tablespoon, in each. Shake each jar for the same time and wait the same time. Only one thing changes: the rice in the jar.
results_table: The salt after 15 minutes: runs freely, forms lumps, or sticks to the glass

materials.item: small glass jars or bottles with lids, washed and completely dry
raw rice from the dabba, 1 cup
a third dry food from the shelf, half a cup: dal, rava, poha or groundnuts
salt, 4 tablespoons
a dry pan and a stove, for the grown-up
a teaspoon, a tablespoon, a half-cup measure and a plate
labels or a marker pen

experiments.safety: A grown-up roasts the salt and lets the pan cool. Do not put the test rice back in the dabba. Wash it and cook it the same day.

schedule.what: Wet half a cup of rice a little and let it dry for 45 minutes. Then shake three lots of grain with dry salt in jars, and read the result.

experiments.record: Draw the three jars. Under each write what is in it, and what the salt did: ran freely, formed lumps, or stuck to the glass.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Rice that was wetted and looks dry
Lumps, and salt stuck to the glass

setup.art: Half a cup of rice spread on a plate with a teaspoon of water being sprinkled over the rice.
setup.caption: 1. Stir 1 teaspoon of water into half a cup of rice. Spread it on a plate for 45 minutes, until it looks dry.

setup.art: A grown-up stirring white salt in a dry pan on a low flame.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up roasts 4 tablespoons of salt in a dry pan for 3 minutes, and lets it cool.

setup.art: Three small glass jars labelled A, B and C, each with rice or grain and a spoonful of salt, and a child shaking one jar.
setup.caption: 3. Put half a cup of grain and 1 tablespoon of dry salt in each jar. Close and shake for 1 minute.

setup.art: A jar tilted on its side with white salt stuck in patches to the inside of the glass, next to a jar where the salt runs loose.
setup.caption: 4. Wait 15 minutes. Tilt each jar. Does the salt run freely, or does it stick?

flow.do: 1. Stir 1 teaspoon of water into half a cup of rice. 2. Spread the rice on a plate. 3. Leave it for 45 minutes, until no grain looks wet. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write them down.
flow.say: I have wetted this rice a little. In 45 minutes it will look dry again. Will it then be the same as the rice in the dabba? How could we find out? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: This rice got a little wet. Soon it will look dry. Will it be the same as before? Why?
flow.parent: The rice soaks up the teaspoon of water and its surface dries. It then looks and feels almost like dabba rice. Do not say whether it is dry inside.
flow.context: This is the first step of Dry Enough. You wet some rice a little and guess what will happen when it looks dry again.

flow.do: While the rice dries, a grown-up roasts 4 tablespoons of salt in a dry pan. Use a low flame for 3 minutes. Tip the salt on to a dry plate, and let it cool for 5 minutes. Dry the three jars with a clean cloth.
flow.say: I am roasting the salt to drive out any damp. The salt must be bone dry for this test. Why do you think that matters?
flow.kid: A grown-up roasts the salt. It must be very dry. Why does that matter?
flow.parent: In the monsoon, salt from the jar is often damp already. Damp salt would stick in every jar and spoil the test.
flow.context: In this step of Dry Enough a grown-up dries the salt by roasting it.

flow.do: Label the jars A, B and C. Put half a cup of dabba rice in A. Put the wetted rice in B. Put the third dry food in C. Add 1 tablespoon of cooled salt to each jar. Close the lids. Your child shakes each jar for 1 minute.
flow.say: Jar A has rice from the dabba. Jar B has the rice we wetted. Jar C has a food you chose from the shelf. Add the salt, close the lids and shake each jar for one minute.
flow.kid: Fill jars A, B and C. Add salt. Close them. Shake each for one minute.

check.q: In Dry Enough, why are the lids kept closed during the wait?
options: So only the grain's damp reaches the salt
So that the rice does not spill
So that the salt stays white
check.why: With the lid on, the only water the salt can take up is water that came out of the grain. An open jar would let in damp room air, and the test would show the weather. If you chose another answer, think about where the salt's water comes from.

flow.context: In this step of Dry Enough you shake three kinds of grain with dry salt in closed jars.

flow.do: Stand the jars for 15 minutes. Then tilt and turn each jar slowly. Look at the salt on the glass and among the grains. Write what you see. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read the note below.
flow.say: Tilt each jar slowly. Does the salt run like dry sand, or does it stick to the glass? Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Tilt each jar. Does the salt run or stick? Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: The wetted rice looked dry. What did the salt show?
good: It still held extra water inside.
Water came out of the rice into the air of the jar.
Looking dry is not the same as being dry.

ask.q: Why does a farmer need this test before filling a grain bin?
good: Damp grain grows mould in the bin.
Some moulds make a poison.
A whole year's grain could be lost.

flow.parent: The reason: grain is always passing water to the air around it, and taking water back. In a closed jar, damp grain makes the air damp. Dry salt takes water out of damp air, turns sticky and clings to the glass. If the salt runs freely, the grain holds less than about 14 or 15 parts of water in 100. That is dry enough to store. Above that, moulds can grow on grain that looks perfectly dry. Wash the test rice and cook it today.
flow.think: Why do many families spread their rice and dal in the sun after the monsoon?
flow.context: This is the last step of Dry Enough. You read the three jars and say what the salt shows about the grain.

activities.title: The Lost Food Hunt: how was each food lost?
activities.context: This is a short activity to start the unit. You look in the kitchen for foods that are past their best. For each one you work out what happened to it.

materials.item: your kitchen shelves, vegetable basket and fridge
a notebook and a pencil
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.safety: Look, and do not taste. Do not sniff anything that has mould on it, because the spores can irritate the nose and chest. Wash your hands at the end.
activities.record: Make a table with three columns: the food, what I see, and what I think happened to it.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up looking into a vegetable basket that holds a sprouting onion and a wrinkled carrot.
setup.caption: 1. Look in the basket, the shelves and the fridge for foods that are past their best.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of three columns and four rows filled in, beside a soft biscuit and a sprouting potato.
setup.caption: 2. For each food, write what you see and what you think happened to it.

flow.do: Ask the question below before you look for anything. Write down the answer.
flow.say: When food at home has to be thrown away, what has usually happened to it? How many different things can go wrong with stored food? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: What goes wrong with food that is kept too long? How many ways can you think of?
flow.parent: Most children say 'it goes bad' or 'germs'. Write down whatever they say. The hunt will add to it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lost Food Hunt. You guess how many ways stored food can be lost.

flow.do: Search together for up to six foods that are past their best. Look for a sprouting onion or potato, limp leaves, a soft biscuit or old nuts. Look for a hard chapati, or insects in atta or rice. For each, your child writes what they see.
flow.say: Find foods that are no longer at their best. Look closely at each one. What do you see? What do you think happened to it?
flow.kid: Find foods that are past their best. Look closely. What happened to each one?
flow.parent: A tidy kitchen may have only two or three. Then ask what your family threw away last week. Old groundnuts or old oil may be smelled from a distance for the sharp, rancid smell. Nothing is tasted.
flow.context: In this step of the Lost Food Hunt you find foods that are past their best. You look at them closely.

flow.do: Read the list together. Sort the foods into groups by what happened to them. Then read out the five ways in the note below, and match each group to one.
flow.say: Sort your foods into groups. Which ones were lost in the same way? How many ways have you found?
flow.kid: Sort your foods into groups. How many ways of being lost did you find?

check.q: An onion in the basket has grown a green shoot. In which way was this onion lost?
options: The onion's own life went on
Microbes ate the onion
Air turned the onion rancid
check.why: An onion is a living bulb, and a shoot means they have begun to grow. No microbe is needed. If you chose microbes, look again: there is no slime, mould or bad smell.
