flow.parent: The five ways: microbes eat the food. The food's own life goes on, as in sprouting, ripening and wilting. Pests get in. Air, light and warmth change the food, as in rancid oil. Water moves in or out, as in a soft biscuit or a hard chapati.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Lost Food Hunt. You sort the foods by the way each was lost.

activities.title: Three Clocks: ten bacteria at three temperatures
activities.context: In this activity you fill in a table and draw a graph. They show how many bacteria ten bacteria become in six hours. You compare a warm kitchen, a cool room and a fridge.

materials.item: a notebook page, or squared paper
a pencil, a ruler and three colour pencils
a calculator, if you want one

activities.record: Draw a table with a row for each hour from 0 to 6, and a column for each place: warm kitchen, cool room and fridge. Then draw a line graph of the first three hours.

setup.art: A notebook table with rows for the hours 0 to 6 and three columns headed warm kitchen, cool room and fridge.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the table. Every place starts with 10 bacteria at hour 0.

setup.art: A child multiplying numbers down the first column, which grows from 10 to 80 to 640.
setup.caption: 2. In the warm kitchen the bacteria double every 20 minutes. That is times 8 each hour.

setup.art: A line graph with one line rising steeply off the top of the page, one rising gently and one lying flat.
setup.caption: 3. Draw the three lines on one graph for the first three hours.

flow.do: Draw the table. Explain the three rules in the note below. Then ask for a guess before any sums are done.
flow.say: Ten bacteria land in a bowl of dal. In a warm kitchen they double every 20 minutes. How many do you think there will be after six hours? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Ten bacteria double every 20 minutes. Guess how many there are after six hours.
flow.parent: The three rules. Warm kitchen, about 35 degrees Celsius: the number doubles every 20 minutes. Cool room, about 18 degrees: it doubles every 2 hours. Fridge, 4 degrees: it stays at 10. These are rounded figures for a common food bacterium, measured in laboratories. Most guesses are far too low.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Clocks. You guess how many bacteria ten bacteria become in six hours.

flow.do: Your child fills in the table. In the warm kitchen, three doublings an hour is times 8. In the cool room the number doubles at hours 2, 4 and 6. The fridge column stays at 10.
flow.say: Fill in the warm kitchen first. Three doublings in an hour is the same as times eight. Then fill in the cool room and the fridge.
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Warm kitchen: times eight each hour. Cool room: double every two hours.
flow.parent: Warm kitchen: 10, 80, 640, 5,120, 40,960, 327,680 and 2,621,440. Cool room: 10 at hour 0, 20 at hour 2, 40 at hour 4 and 80 at hour 6. Fridge: 10 all the way.
flow.context: In this step of Three Clocks you work out the number of bacteria at each hour in three places.

flow.do: Draw a graph for hours 0 to 3, with the side going up to 700. Plot the three lines in three colours. The warm line leaves the page after hour 2. Then ask the questions below.
flow.say: Plot the three lines. What happens to the warm kitchen line? Now look at the table at two hours. Why might the safety rule say two hours?
flow.kid: Draw the three lines. Where does the warm line go? Look at hour two.

ask.q: At two hours the warm kitchen has 640. At six hours it has more than two million. What does that tell you about waiting?
good: Every extra hour makes it eight times worse.
The first hours are small and the later hours are huge.
It is safest to chill food early.

ask.q: Real bacteria wait about an hour before they start to double. How does that change the table?
good: Everything happens an hour later.
At two hours there would be only 80.
It gives us a little more time, which is why the rule is two hours.

check.q: Ten bacteria double every 20 minutes. How many are there after one hour?
check.why: One hour holds three lots of 20 minutes. 10 doubles to 20, then 40, then 80. If you chose 30 or 60, you added or multiplied by three. Doubling three times is times eight.

flow.parent: The waiting time is called the lag time. With a lag of one hour, ten bacteria become about 80 by two hours. That is why two hours in the danger zone is the limit, and one hour on very hot days.
flow.context: This is the last step of Three Clocks. You draw the three lines and find where the two-hour rule comes from.

activities.title: Tiffin Timeline: how many hours does one meal spend warm?
activities.context: In this activity you draw a time line for one real meal, from the stove to the mouth. You count the hours the food spends in the danger zone, between 5 and 60 degrees Celsius.

materials.item: a long strip of paper, or two notebook pages side by side
a pencil, a ruler and a red colour pencil
a lunch box or a meal from your own week to think about

activities.record: Draw the time line with one mark for each hour. Mark when the food was cooked, packed or served, and eaten. Colour the warm hours red and write how many there are.

setup.art: A long strip of paper with hour marks from 6 in the morning to 2 in the afternoon, and small drawings of a stove, a lunch box and a child eating above the marks.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a line with a mark for each hour. Mark when the food was cooked, packed and eaten.

setup.art: The same strip with the stretch from 7 to 1 coloured red and the number 6 written above the stretch.
setup.caption: 2. Colour red every hour the food was neither hot nor cold. Count the red hours.

flow.do: Choose one real meal: a school or office lunch box, food for a journey, or dinner leftovers eaten the next day. Draw the line and mark the three times.
flow.say: Think of one meal that was not eaten straight after cooking. When was it cooked? When was it packed or put away? When was it eaten?
flow.kid: Choose a meal that waited before it was eaten. Mark when it was cooked and eaten.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tiffin Timeline. You draw a time line for one real meal.

flow.do: Colour red each hour in which the food was between hot and cold. Food is out of the danger zone only when it is steaming hot, or in the fridge. Count the red hours. Ask for a guess first.
flow.say: Before we count, guess how many hours this food spent warm. Now colour those hours red and count them. Is it more or less than two?
flow.kid: Guess the warm hours. Colour them red. Count them. More than two?
flow.parent: A lunch box packed at 7 and eaten at 1 has six red hours. Most children are surprised. Do not frighten them. The next step shows why most lunch boxes are still fine.
flow.context: In this step of Tiffin Timeline you count the hours your meal spent in the danger zone.

flow.do: Ask what protected the food during the red hours. Then ask your child for two changes that would cut the red hours or protect the food better.
flow.say: Your lunch spent many hours warm, and you were not ill. What protected it? Now think of two changes that would make it safer still.
flow.kid: What protected your food in the warm hours? Think of two changes to make it safer.

ask.q: What can protect food that must spend hours warm?
good: It is dry, like chapati or roasted sabzi.
It is sour, like lemon rice, tamarind rice or curd rice.
It was cooked fresh that morning, so it started with very few microbes.
The lag time gives an hour or more.

ask.q: What two changes would cut the red hours?
good: A cold pack in the bag.
A flask that keeps food hotter than 60 degrees.
Cook in the morning, not the night before.
Cool the food before closing the lid, so the box is not wet inside.

check.q: Which lunch is the best choice for a box that must wait six hours on a hot day?
options: Lemon rice cooked that morning
Last night's rice with dal
Cut papaya with milk
check.why: Lemon rice is sour and freshly cooked, so it starts with few microbes and holds them back. Last night's rice has already used up its safe hours. Cut fruit and milk are wet and not sour.

flow.context: This is the last step of Tiffin Timeline. You find what protected the food and plan two changes.

activities.title: Two Milks: why one needs the fridge and one does not
activities.context: In this activity you compare a pouch of pasteurised milk with a carton of UHT milk. Then you draw the cold chain that brings the pouch to your home.

materials.item: a pouch of pasteurised milk, or its empty packet
a carton of UHT milk, or the facts in the parent note
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Make a table with two columns, pouch and carton. Write how each was heated, where it is kept, and how long it keeps before and after opening. Under the table, draw the cold chain as a row of linked boxes.

setup.art: A milk pouch and a milk carton side by side on a table, with a child reading the small print on the carton.
setup.caption: 1. Read both packs. Find where to keep each one and how long it lasts.

setup.art: A row of six linked boxes drawn in a notebook: a buffalo, a village cooler, a tanker, a dairy, a delivery van and a home fridge.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the cold chain of the pouch, from the animal to your fridge.

flow.do: Put the two packs side by side. Your child finds on each: the words pasteurised or UHT, the storage instruction and the use-by or best-before date. Ask the question below first.
flow.say: Both of these are milk. One must stay in the fridge and lasts two days. The other sits on a shelf for months. What could make them so different? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One milk needs the fridge. One sits on a shelf for months. What makes them different?
flow.parent: No carton at home? A UHT carton says: store in a cool, dry place. Best before 120 or 180 days. Once opened, keep in the fridge and use within 2 days. Many children guess that a chemical is added. None is.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Milks. You read a milk pouch and a milk carton and compare them.

flow.do: Fill in the table together, using the note below. Then ask what happens to each milk once it is opened.
flow.say: The pouch milk was heated to 72 degrees for 15 seconds. The carton milk was heated to about 140 degrees for a few seconds. Which heating would kill tough spores? What changes when the carton is opened?
flow.kid: Pouch milk was heated to 72 degrees. Carton milk was heated to 140. Which kills spores?

ask.q: Why does an opened carton need the fridge?
good: Microbes from the air and the spout get in.
It is now like any other milk.
The seal was what protected it.

check.q: Why does unopened UHT milk keep for months without a fridge?
options: Nothing alive is inside the sealed carton
A preservative is added
The carton is very cold inside
check.why: UHT heating kills even spores, and the carton is filled without letting any microbe in. Nothing alive is inside to spoil the milk. No preservative is needed.

flow.parent: Pasteurising at 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds kills the microbes that cause disease. Some harmless microbes and spores survive, so the milk needs cold. UHT heating at about 140 degrees for a few seconds kills the spores too.
flow.context: In this step of Two Milks you compare how the two milks were heated and packed.

flow.do: Your child draws the cold chain of the pouch as linked boxes: the animal, the village cooler, the tanker, the dairy, the delivery van, the shop and the home fridge. Ask which link is most likely to break.
flow.say: Draw every cold place the pouch passed through, from the cow or buffalo to our fridge. Which link do you think is the weakest? Why?
flow.kid: Draw every cold place the milk passed through. Which link is the weakest?

ask.q: Which link in the cold chain is most likely to break?
good: The crate outside the shop in the morning sun.
The bag on our doorstep.
The walk home from the shop.

flow.parent: If you can, ask the person who sells your milk how the packets are kept cold on the way. Milk left on a doorstep for two hours in summer has used up its two hours.
flow.context: This is the last step of Two Milks. You draw the cold chain of pouch milk and look for its weakest link.

activities.title: Five at the Table: who needs extra care?
activities.context: In this activity you plan one family meal for five people. Four of them are more easily harmed by unsafe food than you are. You decide what each one can eat as it is, and what must change.

materials.item: a notebook page and a pencil
a ruler, to draw a table

activities.record: Draw a table with five rows for the people and eight columns for the dishes. In each box write a tick, a cross, or the change you would make.

setup.art: A notebook table with five names down the side: baby, pregnant aunt, grandmother, cousin who was ill, and me, with eight dishes along the top.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the table: five people down the side, eight dishes along the top.

setup.art: The same table partly filled with ticks, crosses and short notes such as 'steam first'.
setup.caption: 2. For each person and dish, write a tick, a cross, or the change you would make.

flow.do: Draw the table. The five people: a baby of 8 months, a pregnant aunt, a grandmother of 80, a cousin recovering from typhoid, and your child. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Five people will eat at our table. Who do you think is most easily harmed by unsafe food? What is it about their body that makes you think so?
flow.kid: Five people come to eat. Who is harmed most easily by unsafe food? Why?
flow.parent: The eight dishes: hot idli with sambar. Honey on a dosa. Raw sprouted moong salad. Yesterday's rice from the fridge. Fruit cut at a street stall. Milk that has not been boiled. A soft-boiled egg. Curd rice made this morning.
flow.context: This is the first step of Five at the Table. You guess which people need extra care with food.

flow.do: Your child fills in the table, one dish at a time. For each cross or change, they say the reason. Use the note below to check.
flow.say: Go through the dishes one by one. Who can eat it as it is? Who needs it changed, and how? Who should not have it at all? Tell me the reason each time.
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Tick, cross or write a change. Say the reason each time.
flow.parent: Hot idli with sambar: fine for all. Mash it for the baby, without chilli. Honey: never for a baby under one year. Raw sprouts: steam them for the aunt, the grandmother and the cousin, and give none to the baby. Yesterday's rice: reheat until steaming for the others, and cook fresh food for the baby. Street-cut fruit: cut whole fruit at home for everyone. Unboiled milk: boil it for everyone. Soft-boiled egg: cook it firm for the baby, the aunt, the grandmother and the cousin. Curd rice: fine for all.
flow.context: In this step of Five at the Table you decide what each person can eat, and what must change.

flow.do: Look at the finished table. Ask which dishes were safe for everyone, and what those dishes have in common.
flow.say: Which dishes got a tick for all five people? What do those dishes have in common? What does that tell a cook who has a baby or a grandmother at the table?
flow.kid: Which dishes are safe for all five? What do those dishes share?

ask.q: What do the dishes that are safe for everyone have in common?
good: They are freshly cooked and hot.
They are sour, like curd rice.
Nothing in them is raw or old.

check.q: Why must a baby under one year not be given honey?
options: Honey can hold harmful spores
Honey is too sweet for babies
Babies cannot swallow honey
check.why: Honey can hold the spores of a bacterium. In an older child the gut and its microbes stop the spores. In a baby the spores can grow and make a toxin. If you chose 'too sweet', remember that the rule is about spores, not sugar.

flow.parent: Why these four: a baby has less stomach acid and a small body that loses water fast. A pregnant woman's defences are turned down a little, and some bacteria can reach her baby. Old people and people who have just been ill have weaker defences.
flow.context: This is the last step of Five at the Table. You find what the dishes that are safe for everyone have in common.

projects.title: One Week of Lost Food: measure it, find the causes, change one thing
projects.context: In this seven-day project you record every food your home throws away. You find out how much there is and why it was lost. Then you choose one change in how your family stores food.

materials.item: a sheet of paper stuck on the fridge or the kitchen wall
a pencil on a string
a katori for measuring, or a kitchen scale
a notebook, a ruler and colour pencils for the bar chart

projects.safety: Do not handle mouldy or slimy food. Ask a grown-up to measure it by eye and throw it away.

schedule.what: Make the record sheet, agree what counts, and guess the week's total.
Record each food thrown away: what, how much and why.
Add up the week, draw a bar chart of the causes, and choose one change.

projects.record: A table with five columns: the day, the food, how many katoris, the way it was lost, and the reason behind it. On day 7, a bar chart of katoris for each reason.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a five-column table stuck on a fridge door, with a pencil hanging on a string beside the sheet.
setup.caption: 1. Stick a record sheet on the fridge. Hang a pencil beside the sheet.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a katori of leftover rice over a compost bin while a child writes on the sheet.
setup.caption: 2. Before any food is thrown away, measure it in katoris and write it down.

setup.art: A child drawing a bar chart with bars labelled forgotten, cooked too much, stored in the wrong place and bought too much.
setup.caption: 3. On day 7, add up the katoris and draw a bar for each reason.

flow.do: Day 1. Draw the sheet with five columns. Agree what counts: food that could have been eaten. Peels, seeds, bones and used tea leaves do not count. Ask for a guess, and write it at the top.
flow.say: For one week we will write down every food that could have been eaten and was thrown away. How many katoris do you think it will be? What do you think the biggest reason will be? Why?
flow.kid: Guess how many katoris of food we throw away in a week. Guess the biggest reason.
flow.parent: The 'way' column uses the five ways from the Lost Food Hunt: microbes, the food's own life, pests, air and light, or water moving. The 'reason' column says what led to it: forgotten, cooked too much, bought too much, stored in the wrong place, or left out too long. Tell everyone at home about the sheet.
flow.context: This is day 1 of One Week of Lost Food. You make the record sheet and guess the week's total.

flow.do: Days 2 to 6. Each time food is thrown away, measure it in katoris and fill in a row. Spend five minutes each evening checking the sheet with your child.
flow.say: Before this goes in the bin, how many katoris is it? In which way was it lost? What led to that?
flow.kid: Measure it in katoris. Write the food, the way and the reason.
flow.wait: Do this each day for the next five days
flow.parent: Do not change your family's habits this week, or the record will not be true. Half a katori is fine as a measure. A whole fruit or vegetable counts as one katori.
flow.context: On days 2 to 6 of One Week of Lost Food you record every food your home throws away.

flow.do: Day 7. Add up the katoris. Add them up again for each reason, and draw a bar chart. Compare the total with the guess. Then your child chooses one change to try, and says why it should work.
flow.say: Add up the week. Which reason has the tallest bar? Was your guess close? Now choose one change in how we store or cook food, and tell me why it should work.
flow.kid: Add up the week. Draw the bars. Which is tallest? Choose one change to try.

ask.q: Which change fits your tallest bar?
good: Forgotten food: an eat-me-first shelf in the fridge.
Cooked too much: measure the rice for each person.
Stored in the wrong place: move it to where it keeps.
Left out too long: chill leftovers within two hours.

flow.parent: In many homes the tallest bars are 'forgotten' and 'cooked too much', and microbes only finish the job. The challenge The Eat-Me-First Shelf builds one answer. You can keep the sheet up for a second week to see whether the change worked.
flow.context: This is day 7 of One Week of Lost Food. You add up the week, chart the reasons and choose one change.

challenges.title: Cool the Feast Pot: thick hot food below 43 degrees in 15 minutes
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about cooling cooked food. In Deep or Shallow, the middle of a bowl of hot rice stayed hot for about an hour. Here you design a way to cool the same amount much faster, as a cook for a feast must.
challenges.problem: A cook has thick, hot food that must be kept for tomorrow. The middle must fall below 43 degrees Celsius within 15 minutes, so that it can go into the fridge quickly. Design a way to cool 2 cups of hot cooked rice, or thick upma, that fast.
constraints: Start with 2 cups of food straight from the stove, as in Deep or Shallow.
Nothing may be added to the food: no water and no ice.
The food must stay covered from flies and dust with a clean cloth or a mesh.
Use only things from your kitchen. No fridge and no freezer.
Measure the thickest part with the thermometer at 10 and at 15 minutes. A number on the screen means it is below about 43 degrees Celsius.
materials: 2 cups of hot cooked rice or thick upma for each try
steel plates, trays, bowls and tumblers
a tub or a wide vessel of cold tap water
a hand fan or a table fan
a clean thin cloth or a mesh cover
a digital fever thermometer, washed with soap
general: Spread the food in two or three wide plates, no thicker than a finger.
Stand the plate or vessel in a tub of cold water. Water carries heat away much faster than air.
Stir the food every minute, so that the hot middle keeps coming to the surface.
creative: Use steel and not plastic, because steel passes heat on quickly. Then set the steel plate on a second plate filled with cold water.
Fill a clean steel tumbler with cold water and stand it in the middle of the food. Change the water when it warms.
Press the food into a ring with a hole in the middle. Then no part is far from a surface.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way and test it. Draw your design, write the time it took, and say which part of the design carried the most heat away.

setup.art: A bowl heaped with steaming rice beside a clock, with a child looking at an empty tub, some steel plates and a fan.
setup.caption: 1. You have 2 cups of hot rice and 15 minutes. Plan how to cool the thickest part.

setup.art: Two steel plates of thinly spread rice under a mesh cover, standing in a tub of water, with a thermometer in one plate.
setup.caption: 2. Build your design. Keep the food covered. Measure the thickest part at 10 and at 15 minutes.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Recall Deep or Shallow: the middle of the bowl took about an hour, and the plate took about ten minutes. Ask your child for three ideas, and which they expect to be fastest.
flow.say: In Deep or Shallow, the middle of the bowl stayed hot for about an hour. How could we cool the same rice in fifteen minutes, with nothing added? Which idea will be fastest? Why?
flow.kid: The bowl took an hour to cool. How could you cool it in fifteen minutes?

ask.q: What made the middle of the bowl cool so slowly?
good: It was far from the surface.
The rice does not flow, so the heat had to pass from grain to grain.
Air carries heat away slowly.

flow.context: This is the first step of Cool the Feast Pot. You think of ways to cool thick hot food fast.

flow.do: Your child chooses one design and sets out the plates, the water tub, the fan and the cover. Nothing is hot yet.
flow.say: Choose one design. Set everything out before the rice comes, because the clock starts when I serve it.
flow.kid: Choose your design. Set everything out before the hot rice comes.
flow.context: In this step of Cool the Feast Pot you set out your design before the hot food arrives.

flow.do: A grown-up serves 2 cups of hot rice into the design, and the clock starts. Take a reading in the thickest part at 10 and at 15 minutes. Write each one down.
flow.say: The clock starts now. Do what your design needs. At ten and at fifteen minutes we measure the thickest part.
flow.kid: The clock starts. Work your design. Measure the thickest part at ten and fifteen minutes.
flow.parent: A grown-up handles the hot rice for the first five minutes. Water must not splash into the food. If the screen shows a number at 10 minutes, the design has done very well.
flow.context: In this step of Cool the Feast Pot you test your design with hot food and take three readings.

flow.do: Compare the time with Deep or Shallow. Ask the questions below. If there is time, change one thing and try again.
flow.say: Did the thickest part fall below 43 degrees in fifteen minutes? Which part of your design carried the most heat away? What would you change for a pot of thirty kilos?
flow.kid: Did you beat fifteen minutes? What carried the most heat away? What would you change?

ask.q: How would a wedding cook use your idea for 30 kilograms of dal?
good: Divide it into many shallow trays.
Stand the trays in a trough of cold water.
Stir it with a clean paddle.

flow.parent: Kitchens that cook for hundreds do exactly these things: shallow trays, cold water baths and stirring. The cooled rice is safe to eat, since far less than two hours have passed.
flow.context: This is the last step of Cool the Feast Pot. You compare your time with the bowl in Deep or Shallow and improve your design.

challenges.title: The Eat-Me-First Shelf: make sure no food is forgotten
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about storing food at home. In many homes, food is thrown away because it was forgotten at the back of the fridge. Here you design a way to make the food that must be eaten soonest the easiest to see.
challenges.problem: Food gets pushed to the back when new food arrives, and it is found again when it has spoiled. Shops solve this with a rule called first in, first out: the oldest stock is sold first. Design a system for your own fridge and shelves. It must lead everyone at home to eat the oldest and most perishable food first.
constraints: It must work for everyone at home, including someone who was not told about it.
It must take less than one minute a day to keep going.
It must show the date on every leftover.
It must use only things you have: boxes, paper, tape, a marker pen, rubber bands.
Raw fish, meat and eggs stay on the lowest shelf, below cooked food, whatever the system.
materials: your fridge and one kitchen shelf
a box or a tray that fits on a fridge shelf
paper, sticky tape and a marker pen
general: Mark one box or one shelf 'Eat me first', at eye level, and put leftovers and opened packets there.
Write the date on a piece of tape on every leftover box.
When new food comes, move the older food to the front and put the new food behind.
creative: Put a red rubber band on anything that must be eaten today. Take the band off when it is eaten.
Keep a dated list on the fridge door of what is inside. Cross food off as it is eaten.
Plan one 'clear the fridge' meal each week, such as a mixed vegetable kootu or fried rice.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own system and set it up. Draw it, explain it to your family in three sentences, and run it for one week.

setup.art: An open fridge crowded with boxes, with a small covered bowl hidden at the back behind a milk packet.
setup.caption: 1. Look for the places where food hides and gets forgotten.

setup.art: The same fridge with a tray at eye level marked 'Eat me first', holding three boxes with dates written on tape.
setup.caption: 2. Make the oldest food the easiest to see. Put a date on every leftover.

flow.do: Open the fridge and one shelf together. Your child finds the three oldest foods, and the places where food is hard to see. Ask the question below.
flow.say: Find the three oldest foods here. How did you know they were the oldest? Where does food hide in our kitchen?
flow.kid: Find the three oldest foods. How do you know? Where does food hide?

ask.q: Why is the oldest food usually at the back?
good: New food is put in front of it.
Nobody moves the old food forward.
Small boxes hide behind big ones.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Eat-Me-First Shelf. You look for the oldest foods and the places where food is forgotten.

flow.do: Your child designs the system on paper, then builds it: a marked box or shelf, dates on tape, and a rule for where new food goes. Check it against the five limits in the problem.
flow.say: Draw your system first. Then build it. I will check it against the five limits. Would a visitor understand it without being told?
flow.kid: Draw your system. Build it. Would a visitor understand it?
flow.parent: Keep raw fish, meat and eggs on the lowest shelf even if they are the oldest. A note on the eat-me-first box can point to them.
flow.context: In this step of the Eat-Me-First Shelf you design and build your system.

flow.do: Your child explains the system to someone else at home in three sentences. Then ask the question below, and agree a day next week to check how it worked.
flow.say: Explain your system to the family in three sentences. How will we know in a week whether it worked?
flow.kid: Explain your system in three sentences. How will you know it worked?

ask.q: How will you know whether the system worked?
good: Less food is thrown away than in One Week of Lost Food.
Nothing in the fridge is older than two days without a date.
People use the box without being reminded.

check.q: The fridge holds half a packet of older milk. Where does a new packet of milk go?
options: Behind the older packet
In front of the older packet
On the counter
check.why: First in, first out means the older milk is used first, so it must be the easier one to reach. If you chose 'in front', the older milk would be hidden and forgotten.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Eat-Me-First Shelf. You explain your system and plan how to check that it works.

worksheets.title: How food is lost, and where it keeps

items.p: A biscuit left open in the monsoon turns soft. In which way was it lost?
opts: Water moved in from the air
The biscuit's own life went on
items.why: A dry biscuit takes in water from damp air and turns soft. No microbe is needed. Microbes would leave mould, slime or a bad smell.

items.p: Match each sign to the way the food was lost.
pairs: The food's own life went on
A sharp smell from old oil
items.why: Each way of losing food leaves its own sign. Reading the sign tells you which kind of storage would have saved the food.

items.p: The fine threads that make up the body of a mould are called ____.
items.why: Hyphae grow into the food, much deeper than the fuzzy patch on top. This is why soft food with one mould spot is thrown away whole.

items.p: Food that looks and smells fine is always safe to eat.
items.why: False. Spoilage microbes change the look and smell. Many harmful bacteria and toxins change nothing. Safety depends on how warm the food was kept, and for how long.

items.p: Which microbes are most likely to spoil a bowl of wet cooked rice first?
items.why: Bacteria multiply fastest on wet food that is not sour. Moulds are slower, and they win only on drier or sourer food. Weevils are insects, and they eat dry grain.

items.p: Sort these foods by the place where each keeps best.
items.why: Cooked dal and milk are perishable, so they need cold. Rice and atta are lost to damp and pests, so they need a dry, sealed place. Potatoes and onions are alive, so they need dark and moving air.

items.p: Freezing kills the microbes in food.
items.why: False. Freezing stops microbes from multiplying, but most stay alive. They start again when the food thaws.

items.p: Why is cooked food cooled in shallow vessels?
opts: Every part is near the surface
The fridge holds more of them
items.why: Heat leaves food only through the surface. In a shallow layer no part is far from the surface, so the whole of the food cools fast.

items.p: The range of temperature from about 5 to 60 degrees Celsius is called the ____ zone.
items.why: Bacteria multiply in the danger zone, fastest between 20 and 45 degrees Celsius. Cooked food should spend no more than about two hours there.

items.p: In Deep or Shallow, the plate rice cooled long before the middle of the bowl. Explain why.
items.a: Heat leaves rice only through the surface. On the plate every grain is near the surface. In the bowl, heat from the middle must pass from grain to grain to reach the outside. That is slow.
items.why: A strong answer says where heat leaves. It compares how far the heat must travel on the plate and in the bowl.

items.p: A family cooks dal at 1 o'clock and eats it again at 8. Write what they should do in between.
items.a: Put the leftover dal in a shallow covered vessel. Get it into the fridge by 3 o'clock, which is within two hours. At 8, reheat only what they will eat until it bubbles, and stir the middle.
items.why: A strong answer has three parts: cool it fast, chill it within two hours, and reheat it until steaming.

items.p: Draw a slice of bread cut through, with a mould growing on it. Label the hyphae and the spores.
items.a: A fuzzy patch on top of the slice. Fine threads, the hyphae, run from the patch down into the bread. Small coloured dots on stalks above the patch hold the spores.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the hyphae reach deeper than the patch you can see.
items.art: An outline of a slice of bread seen from the side, with blank label lines.

items.p: Should hot leftover dal go straight into the fridge?

views.who: A grandmother who cooks for the family
views.says: No. Hot food warms the fridge and the milk beside it. Let it cool on the counter first.
Yes, in a shallow box. On the counter it can spend hours in the danger zone.
It depends on the amount. A katori can go in warm. A big pot must be divided and stood in cold water first.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For the officer: bacteria double every 20 minutes in warm food. For the grandmother: a big hot pot does warm a fridge. A strong answer may say that the amount of food decides.
items.why: This is a real disagreement between kitchens and food safety agencies. A strong answer uses the two-hour rule and says what a big pot does to a fridge.

items.p: Put these in order, from the food that keeps for the shortest time to the longest.
items: Dry rice in an airtight bin
a: Dry rice in an airtight bin
items.why: Warm, wet dal lasts about two hours. Cold, sour curd lasts about a week. Onions last about two months, and dry rice about two years. Dryness protects longest.

items.p: Who needs the most care with food at a family meal?
items.why: A baby has less stomach acid, defences that are still learning, and a small body that loses water fast. The other three are healthy and well past babyhood.

items.p: Ten bacteria double every 20 minutes. How many are there after 2 hours?
items.why: Two hours hold six lots of 20 minutes. 10 doubles to 20, 40, 80, 160, 320 and 640.

items.p: Bacteria wait before they start to multiply in new food. What is this wait called?
items.why: The lag time is the wait before doubling begins. Doubling time is how long one doubling takes once they have started.

items.p: Dal sat out for one hour at lunch and one hour at dinner. Why do the two hours add up?
items.a: The bacteria that multiplied at lunch are still in the dal. The fridge only stopped them for a while. At dinner they go on doubling from where they stopped.
items.why: A strong answer says that cold pauses bacteria and does not remove them, so the count carries on.

items.p: Boiling food and covering it stops every microbe from growing in it later.
items.why: False. The spores of some bacteria survive boiling. They wake when the food cools to a warm temperature. A lid keeps flies out, but it does not cool the food.

items.p: Three of these foods are perishable. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Milk, cut papaya and cooked rice are wet and not sour, so they spoil within hours in the warmth. Dry toor dal has no free water and keeps for about a year.

items.p: Match each person to the reason they need extra care with food.
pairs: Little stomach acid and a small body
Some bacteria can reach her baby
The body is still weak from illness
items.why: Each of these people can fall ill from fewer microbes than a healthy child or adult. So their food is cooked fully and served fresh.

items.p: A power cut lasts 3 hours and the fridge door stays shut. What about the milk inside?
opts: It is still cold enough to keep
items.why: A closed fridge stays cold for about four hours. Opening the door lets the cold air out, so the door stays shut.

items.p: In Three Sealed Bags, wet rice turned slimy and bread turned fuzzy. Explain why they spoiled differently.
items.a: Different microbes won on each food. Bacteria need plenty of free water, and they made the slime on the wet rice. Bread is too dry for most bacteria, so slower moulds grew on it as fuzzy threads.
items.why: A strong answer names the microbe for each food. It says why that food suits that microbe.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one kill most microbes, or only stop them from multiplying?
items.why: Heat kills. Cold and dryness only take away what microbes need to multiply. When the food warms up or gets wet, the microbes start again.

items.p: A wedding cook finds that 30 kilograms of boiled dal stayed warm all night. Should she serve it?

views.says: No. Nobody can see or smell what grew in it, and 600 guests will eat it.

views.who: The family paying for the wedding
views.says: Yes. It was boiled and covered, it smells fine, and it cost four thousand rupees.
No. Babies and old people are here, and boiling it again may not remove every toxin.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. Against serving: the middle of a big pot stays in the danger zone all night, and some toxins survive heat. For serving: food is precious, and nobody can show that this dal is unsafe. A strong answer weighs who would be harmed.
items.why: This is a real choice that cooks face. A strong answer uses the science of cooling, and is honest that nobody can be sure about this one pot.

items.p: A tin with a swollen lid holds ____ made by living microbes.
items.why: Microbes inside a tin make gas as they feed, and the gas pushes the lid out. The food in such a tin must never be opened or tasted.

items.p: A deep pot of hot dal has stood for two hours. Label the hottest part and the coolest part.
a: Hottest part: the middle of the pot, far from every surface
Coolest part: the top and the sides, where heat leaves
items.why: Heat leaves only at the surface, so the outside cools first and the middle cools last.
items.art: A deep cooking pot drawn cut in half from top to bottom, full of dal, with two blank label lines.

items.p: Why does pouch milk need a fridge, while unopened UHT carton milk does not?
opts: A pouch is thinner than a carton
items.why: Pasteurising at 72 degrees Celsius kills the microbes that cause disease, but some others and their spores survive. UHT heating kills the spores too, and the carton lets no microbe in.

items.p: Reheating leftover food once, until it steams in the middle, is a safe habit.
items.why: True, if the food was chilled within two hours. Steaming heat in the middle kills the bacteria that grew slowly in the fridge. Reheating again and again gives them more warm hours.

items.p: A lunch box is packed at 7 and eaten at 1. Give two ways to make that lunch safer.
items.a: Choose a dry or sour food, such as chapati with dry sabzi, lemon rice or curd rice. Cook it that morning, not the night before. Add a cold pack, or use a flask that keeps food very hot.
items.why: A strong answer gives two changes. Each one cuts the warm hours, or makes the food harder for bacteria to grow in.

items.p: In Dry Enough, salt stuck to the glass in the jar of wetted rice. Explain where the water came from.
items.a: The water came out of the rice. The rice looked dry, but it still held extra water inside. In the closed jar that water passed into the air, and the dry salt took it up and turned sticky.
items.why: A strong answer traces the water from the rice, to the air in the jar, to the salt.

items.p: Why does a mould poison still matter after the mouldy food is cooked?
opts: Cooking does not destroy the poison
The mould hides from the heat
items.why: Aflatoxin and some other mould poisons survive roasting and boiling. The heat kills the mould, but the poison the mould made stays in the food.

items.p: A bowl cools in 1 hour. At double the width it takes 4 hours. And at 4 times the width?
items.why: Four times as wide is twice as wide, and then twice as wide again. So the time is 4 times 4, which is 16 hours.

items.p: Rice that was cooled fast, chilled, and reheated once until steaming is safe to eat.
items.why: True. The danger with rice is the warm hours before it is chilled. Rice that was cooled fast gave the spores no time to multiply.

items.p: Put these in order, as raw milk spoils in a warm place.
items: Protein-eating bacteria make the milk smell rotten
Yeasts and moulds use up the acid
The milk turns sour and sets
a: The milk turns sour and sets
Yeasts and moulds use up the acid
Protein-eating bacteria make the milk smell rotten
items.why: Each kind of microbe changes the milk, and the change suits the next kind. Scientists call such a line of changes a succession.

items.p: Is cooked rice left overnight in water safe to eat?

views.says: Yes. My family has eaten pakhala every summer for generations. It cools the body, and it has never made us ill.
No. Cooked rice at room temperature for twelve hours breaks the two-hour rule, and spores are common on rice.

views.who: A scientist who studies fermented food
views.says: Perhaps. The water turns sour as helpful bacteria grow, and sourness holds back many harmful ones. But it needs clean water and a clean pot, and few studies have measured it.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say what test would help to settle the question.
items.a: Any view with a reason. A strong answer sees that the rule and the tradition may both be right. The sour water changes what can grow. A useful test: measure the sourness and count the harmful bacteria in many pots, at several room temperatures.
items.why: Scientists have not settled this. A strong answer respects long experience, respects the rule, and says what evidence is missing.

items.p: Birds on many farms fall ill. How could you find out whether a germ or the feed is the cause?
items.a: Find out what all the ill flocks have in common. If they share one batch of feed, and flocks on other feed stay well, the feed is suspected. Then give that feed to a few healthy birds and see whether they fall ill. If a germ were the cause, ill birds would pass the illness to healthy birds beside them.
items.why: A strong answer compares ill and healthy flocks, and then tests the suspected cause directly.

items.p: Weevils are sealed inside an airtight bin of grain. What happens over the next weeks?
opts: The oxygen runs low and they stop feeding
items.why: The insects and the grain use up the oxygen in the sealed bin. With too little oxygen the weevils stop feeding and die. Farmers store grain in sealed bags for this reason.

items.p: Shops sell the oldest stock first. This rule is called first in, first ____.
items.why: First in, first out means the food that arrived first is used first. At home, older food goes to the front and new food behind it.

items.p: Draw the cold chain for a pouch of milk, from the animal to your fridge. Mark the weakest link.
items.a: A row of linked boxes: the cow or buffalo, the village cooler, the tanker, the dairy, the delivery van, the shop and the home fridge. The weakest link is often the crate outside the shop or the bag on the doorstep.
items.why: A strong drawing shows every link, and gives a reason for the link marked as weakest.
items.art: A row of seven empty boxes joined by arrows, with a milk pouch drawn at the right-hand end.

items.p: Match each observation to what it shows.
pairs: Salt sticks in a jar of rice that looks dry
Looking dry is not the same as being dry

items.why: Each observation is evidence, and each conclusion says only what that evidence supports.

items.p: Why does a nose warn you about spoiled food, but not about the most harmful microbes?
items.a: A nose picks up the acids and gases that huge numbers of spoilage microbes make. Many harmful bacteria make people ill in small numbers, and they make no smell. Some leave a toxin that has no smell either.
items.why: A strong answer separates spoilage, which makes smells, from harm, which may make none.

items.p: Which storage place suits potatoes best?
items.why: Potatoes are alive. Light turns them green, and the green part holds a poison called solanine. A sealed bag traps damp, so they rot. Freezing breaks their cells.

items.p: On a day hotter than 32 degrees Celsius, cooked food should be chilled within one hour.
items.why: True. Bacteria double faster as food gets warmer. So food safety agencies shorten the two-hour rule to one hour on very hot days.

items.p: A home throws away 2 katoris of food each day. How many katoris is that in 4 weeks?
items.why: Four weeks are 28 days. 28 times 2 is 56 katoris.

quiz.p: A packet of groundnuts kept for a year smells sharp and stale. What happened?
opts: Air and warmth turned the oil rancid
quiz.why: The oil in nuts slowly changes in air, light and warmth, and smells rancid. Dry nuts hold too little water for bacteria.

quiz.p: How do microbes eat solid food?
opts: They digest it outside their bodies
They wait for it to melt
quiz.why: A microbe has no mouth. Enzymes cut the food outside the microbe's body, and the small pieces pass in. The leftovers are the sourness, smell and slime of spoiled food.

quiz.p: Which food is most likely to grow fuzzy mould, and not slime?
quiz.why: Bread is too dry for most bacteria, so moulds spoil it. Dal, milk and fish curry are wet and not sour, so bacteria get there first.

quiz.p: Why can cooked food stay out for only about two hours?
opts: Bacteria in warm food keep doubling
Flies need two hours to find it
quiz.why: In warm food some bacteria double every 20 minutes. After a short wait, their numbers rise faster and faster.

quiz.p: Two cups of hot rice are pressed into a deep bowl. Which part cools last?
quiz.why: Heat leaves only through the surface. The middle is farthest from every surface, so its heat has the longest way to go.

quiz.p: A large pot of hot sambar should go into the fridge whole, with the lid on.
quiz.why: False. The middle of a large pot stays warm for hours, even in a fridge. Divide the sambar into shallow vessels first.

quiz.p: Where should atta be stored in the monsoon?
opts: In a paper bag near the sink
quiz.why: Atta takes in damp from monsoon air, and damp atta grows mould and draws insects. An airtight dabba keeps the damp out.

quiz.p: Which of these must a baby under one year never be given?
quiz.why: Honey can hold spores that grow in a baby's gut and make a toxin. The other three are safe foods for a baby.

quiz.p: Which meal needs the most care?
opts: Sambar for 200 guests, cooked the night before
Hot dosas eaten straight off the tawa
quiz.why: A large amount cooked hours ahead cools slowly, and many people will eat it. The other three are fresh and hot, or protected by a peel, or dry.

quiz.p: In a fair test of how two vessels cool hot food, what must be different?
opts: Only the shape of the vessel
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing and keeps the rest the same. Then any difference in the result comes from that one thing.

quiz.p: Groundnuts stored damp grow a mould. Why is roasting them not enough?
opts: The mould's poison survives the heat
quiz.why: The mould makes a poison called aflatoxin. Roasting kills the mould, but the poison stays. Mouldy and shrivelled nuts are thrown away.

applications: Cooks for weddings, temples, gurdwaras and school meals divide hot food into shallow trays. Or they cook it close to serving time.
Dairy cooperatives chill milk in village coolers within hours of milking, so that it reaches the city fresh.
Farmers dry grain in the sun and test its dampness before they fill a bin or a godown.
Sealed three-layer grain bags let farmers keep grain and pulses for a year with no insect poison.
Shops and home kitchens use first in, first out, so that the oldest food is used first.
Hospitals and baby-care centres cook food fresh for patients and babies, and serve no raw sprouts or raw milk.
Vaccines travel in a cold chain of their own, in ice boxes, to every village health centre.

open_questions.q: How does a resting spore in cooked food sense that it is time to wake up?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that warmth and certain nutrients start the waking. They do not fully know why some spores in the same food wake early and others wait for days.

open_questions.q: Is cooked rice soaked overnight in water safe, and does it do the body good?
open_questions.why_open: Millions of people in India eat it. The water turns sour, which should hold back many harmful bacteria. But few careful studies have counted the microbes in real kitchens.

open_questions.q: Will hotter summers bring more illness from food?
open_questions.why_open: Records from several countries show more food poisoning in warmer weeks. Nobody knows how far better fridges and better habits will cancel this out.

open_questions.q: Can viruses that attack only bacteria be used to protect stored food?
open_questions.why_open: Such viruses are called bacteriophages. A few are already used on some foods. Scientists are still testing how well they work and how fast bacteria become able to resist them.

open_questions.q: Do vegetables in a fridge keep a daily rhythm, and does that change how good they are for us?
open_questions.why_open: In 2013 cabbages from a shop were found to keep a rhythm of day and night. Nobody yet knows whether storing vegetables in light and dark would make them more nourishing.

maths.problem: In Deep or Shallow, the plate rice fell below 43 degrees Celsius after 10 minutes. The middle of the bowl took 60 minutes. How many times as long did the middle of the bowl take?
maths.explain: 60 divided by 10 is 6. So the middle of the bowl stayed hot 6 times as long as the rice on the plate.
maths.context: In Deep or Shallow you time how long heaped rice and spread rice stay hotter than 43 degrees Celsius. These are made-up times.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one time by the other shows how much the shape of the rice changed the cooling.

maths.problem: Ten bacteria double every 20 minutes. How many are there after 3 hours?
maths.explain: Three hours hold 9 lots of 20 minutes. Doubling 10 nine times gives 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, 640, 1,280, 2,560 and 5,120.
maths.context: In Three Clocks you fill in a table of how many bacteria ten bacteria become in a warm kitchen.
maths.why_maths: A doubling pattern grows far faster than most people guess. Writing it out shows why an extra hour matters so much.

maths.problem: In a warm kitchen bacteria double every 20 minutes. In a cool room they double every 2 hours. Each place starts with 10. After 4 hours, how many times as many are in the warm kitchen?
maths.explain: In 4 hours the warm kitchen has 12 doublings, which gives 40,960. The cool room has 2 doublings, which gives 40. 40,960 divided by 40 is 1,024.
maths.context: In Three Clocks you compare how fast bacteria multiply in a warm kitchen and in a cool room.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two totals shows that a small change in doubling time makes a very large change in the number.

maths.problem: Thick food in a pot twice as wide takes about 4 times as long to cool in the middle. The middle of a small vessel cools in 3 hours. A big vessel is twice as wide. Will its middle be cool 9 hours later?
maths.explain: 4 times 3 hours is 12 hours. After 9 hours the middle of the big vessel is still warm.
maths.context: In Deep or Shallow you find that the middle of a heap of rice cools last. This problem uses the rule for a bigger pot.
maths.why_maths: The sum lets a cook predict what is happening in the middle of a pot, where nobody can see.

maths.problem: The power goes off at 1:30 in the afternoon and comes back at 7:10 in the evening. A closed fridge stays cold for about 4 hours. For about how long was the fridge too warm?
maths.explain: From 1:30 to 7:10 is 5 hours and 40 minutes. Take away the 4 cold hours. That leaves 1 hour and 40 minutes in the danger zone, which is inside the two-hour rule.
maths.context: In Serve, Change or Stop, two cards are about food in a fridge during a power cut.
maths.why_maths: Working out the warm time tells you whether the food is still inside the two-hour rule.

maths.problem: In One Week of Lost Food, a family recorded 20 katoris. 9 were forgotten and 6 were cooked too much. 3 were stored in the wrong place and 2 were left out too long. What percentage was forgotten?
maths.explain: 9 out of 20 is the same as 45 out of 100. So 45 per cent of the lost food was forgotten.
maths.context: In One Week of Lost Food you record every food your home throws away, and the reason. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: A percentage shows which reason matters most, so the family knows which habit to change first.

maths.problem: A home throws away 2 katoris of cooked food a day. One katori costs about 12 rupees to buy and cook. What does the lost food cost in a year of 365 days?
maths.explain: 2 katoris a day cost 24 rupees. 24 times 365 is 8,760 rupees in a year.
maths.context: In One Week of Lost Food you measure the food your home throws away in katoris. This problem turns katoris into rupees.
maths.why_maths: A small daily loss is easy to ignore. Multiplying it over a year shows what it really costs.

how_we_found_out.context: This is the true story of how scientists found a poison made by a mould in stored groundnuts. It began with farm birds in England in 1960.
how_we_found_out.story: In the summer of 1960, young turkeys began to die on farms in the south and east of England. About 100,000 birds died within a few months. Farmers and vets thought a new germ was passing from bird to bird. They named the illness Turkey X disease. But no germ could be found, and sick birds did not make healthy birds ill. A poultry adviser, William Blount, looked at what the sick flocks had eaten. Their feed all held groundnut meal from one shipment from Brazil. Scientists fed that meal to healthy ducklings, and the ducklings fell ill. In 1961 Kenneth Sargeant and his team in London found a mould growing in the meal. The mould is called Aspergillus flavus. They showed that the mould makes a poison, which was named aflatoxin. The groundnuts had grown mouldy in damp storage. In 1974 the same poison harmed people in about 200 villages of Gujarat and Rajasthan. Rain had wet their maize, and the maize had grown mouldy. Doctors from Hyderabad traced the illness to the maize.
how_we_found_out.who: William Blount, a poultry adviser in England. Kenneth Sargeant and his team at the Tropical Products Institute in London. K. A. V. R. Krishnamachari, Ramesh Bhat and their team at the National Institute of Nutrition in Hyderabad.
how_we_found_out.when: The turkeys died in 1960. The mould was found in 1961, and the poison was named soon after. The outbreak in western India was in 1974.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the turkeys had an infectious disease, caused by a new germ that passed from bird to bird. Tracing the feed showed that only birds fed one batch of groundnut meal fell ill. Feeding that meal to healthy ducklings made them ill too.
how_we_found_out.art: A farm worker in the 1960s holding a scoop of brown groundnut meal over a feed trough, with young turkeys behind a wire fence and a sack marked with a ship's stamp.

roots.context: In this unit you timed how long the middle of a heap of hot rice stayed hot. Here we ask what that test says about food, about microbes and about your own body.

deep_truth.truth: In Deep or Shallow, the spread rice cooled in minutes, but the middle of the heap stayed hot. Heat leaves food only through the surface, and the middle of a heap is far from the surface. Microbes multiply fastest in food that stays warm for hours. So the shape and size of a heap of food help decide how safe the food stays.
deep_truth.habit: We think that safety is inside the food: it is clean or dirty, fresh or stale, cooked or raw. But two helpings of the same rice from the same pot can end up different. What happens to food also depends on its shape, its size and the hours it has spent warm.
deep_truth.evidence: In Deep or Shallow, rice from one pot was put on a plate and in a bowl. The plate rice fell below 43 degrees Celsius in about ten minutes. The middle of the bowl took about an hour. Outbreaks at feasts are often traced to food that cooled slowly in big vessels.

three.who_am_i: You are a warm body with a surface too. A baby is small, with a lot of skin for their size, so they cool fast. You make heat all day and lose it through your skin.
three.what_is_life: A bacterium is so small that every part of them is close to their surface. Food gets in quickly and waste gets out quickly. That is one reason the smallest living beings multiply the fastest.
three.what_is_this_world: The same rule works for a planet. The Earth is so big that its middle is still hot after four and a half billion years. A small asteroid cooled long ago.

roots.thread: The rice on the plate and the rice in the bowl were the same rice, with the same few spores. Nothing about the rice made one safer than the other. The difference lay in how far each grain was from the air. So what happens to a thing depends on what it is made of. It also depends on how the thing meets the world around it. Many sages taught that nothing exists by itself, apart from everything else. The science here shows one exact case. The middle of a heap is what it is because of all the rice around it.

teachings.teaching: The verse lists the foods that a dull and heavy mind prefers. The first food on the list is food cooked more than one watch ago. A watch is about three hours.
teachings.link: The verse sets a time limit on cooked food. The limit is close to the two-hour rule of food safety. The Gita is speaking about the mind and its qualities. It does not speak about microbes, which nobody had seen.

teachings.source: J. B. S. Haldane, the essay 'On Being the Right Size' (1926)
teachings.teaching: A change in size changes what a body can do. An elephant has far less skin for each kilogram of body than a mouse has. So the elephant loses heat slowly, and the mouse must eat all day to stay warm.
teachings.link: Haldane wrote about mice and elephants. The same rule makes a wedding pot cool more slowly than a katori. Haldane later lived and worked in Kolkata and Bhubaneswar.

teachings.source: Charaka Samhita, Vimana Sthana, chapter 1, the rules for eating
teachings.teaching: Eat food while it is warm, in the right amount, and only after the last meal is digested.
teachings.link: Food that is still warm from the fire has had no time in the danger zone. Charaka gave the rule for good digestion. The link to microbes is ours.

science.text: Heat leaves a body only through its surface. A body twice as wide has four times the surface and eight times the volume. So it holds its heat longer.
The Earth's middle is still hot. Part of the heat is left from the Earth's making, and part is made inside by radioactive atoms. Scientists still argue about how much comes from each.
How a resting spore in cooked food senses that it is time to wake is only partly understood.

other_view.view: Shape and size matter only for big pots. In a home kitchen, most illness from food comes from dirty water, unwashed hands and raw food touching cooked food. Clean food eaten fresh is safe in any vessel. Putting the shape of the heap at the centre makes a small part of food safety look like the whole.

practice.title: Where the warmth leaves
practice.say: Hold a tumbler of warm water in both hands. Close your eyes and breathe slowly. Feel the warmth pass into your palms. Your palms are the outside world for the water. Now put the tumbler down and hold your own bare arm. You are warm too, and your warmth is leaving through your skin right now. Sit for five breaths and feel it go.
practice.kid: Hold a warm tumbler in both hands. Feel the warmth go into your palms. Now hold your own arm. Your warmth is leaving through your skin. Sit still for five breaths.

ask: In Deep or Shallow, the plate rice and the bowl rice came from one pot. After an hour they were different. What made the difference: the rice, the vessel or the time?
You are warm and you have a surface, like the heap of rice. In what ways are you like the heap, and in what ways are you different?
The hours that a food has spent warm leave no mark on it. How much of what matters about a thing is its past, which nobody can see?

playtest: The experiments, activities and games were reasoned through step by step, as a family in a flat would do them. They have not yet been tried at home. Deep or Shallow (core) needs freshly cooked rice and a digital fever thermometer. Most such thermometers show HI above about 43 degrees Celsius, and some show a number up to 45. So the first step checks yours. The times will differ from home to home with the bowl and the room. The plate should show a number within about 15 minutes. The middle of a full 2-cup bowl should stay at HI far longer. Rice straight from the cooker may harm a fever thermometer. So the edge of the bowl is measured only from 20 minutes, and the middle from 40 minutes. A home with no thermometer uses steam and a grown-up's finger. A grown-up handles the rice for the first ten minutes. Three Sealed Bags (core) takes six days and the bags are never opened. In warm weather the wet rice should change first and turn slimy. The bread should grow fuzzy mould after three to five days. The lemon may show nothing for a week, and the step says to wait longer. In winter everything is slower. A child with asthma or a mould allergy only watches. Dry Enough needs salt that has been roasted dry, and jars that are completely dry. It is a farmers' test.
